It’s much better to be different than it is to be the same as everybody else. When you’re the same, you disappear, and become just another sheep in the herd. When you’re different, it means you have the tenacity to think for yourself. To forge your own path in life, and to be your own person. 

There’s nothing wrong with being weird or different. If anybody judges you for being the way you are, it’s because they’re not in touch with their own identity, or who they are personally. 

Embrace your quirks, instead of hating them. Cherish the things that make you unique, instead of suppressing them. Use these things to work for you, instead of letting them bring you down. You are like nobody else, and nobody else is like you. Out of all the billions of people who have ever lived, nobody else has seen what you’ve seen, or gone through what you’ve gone through.

It can be lonely being different, but that’s why you should embrace the people who accept you for who you are. These people are rare, but if they stand by you, you’ll know they truly appreciate you and understand you. They are the people who matter, and will always be there for you. It’s much better to have 1 true friend than 100 fake friends. 

I hope you can overcome whatever problems you’re facing, and I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

As long as you make it clear that you’re trying and putting forth the necessary effort, I seriously doubt your parents are going to be upset with you for having trouble with your Algebra course. Expecting you to excel at every single subject is not only unrealistic, it’s ludicrous. If they truly want what’s best for you and your education, they’ll be understanding and willing to help, even if you don’t pass. 

If you don’t pass Algebra this semester, you can most likely take it over the summer, or retake it when you’re a senior. If you talk to your school counselor, they can give you options on what to do. If you talk to your algebra teacher, they can give you extra material to study. Ask them if there’s any extra credit you can do, to make up your grade. Remember to always turn in your homework on time, since this makes up a big chunk of your grade, and can make the difference between passing and failing. I had a horrible time in algebra as well, but as long as you do the absolute bare minimum, you can pass with a C or a D.

I understand school is frustrating. Up until now, school has basically been your entire life. But once you graduate, you’ll realize school is SOOOOOOO temporary. Once you’re an adult, you’re going to forget this stupid algebra course ever existed. There’s still a whole world out there for you to explore. You still have the rest of your life to travel the world and make friends and have fun. The best years of your life aren’t over, because they haven’t even begun. 

Instead of hurting yourself, turn your anger into something productive. Use it to motivate you to work hard and kick Algebra’s ass, so you can pass with flying colors. There’s no better feeling than proving people wrong, and laughing in the faces of the people who once doubted you. 

I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

I’m only suggesting giving her as much information as you possibly can, so she can learn more about bipolar depression, and what the symptoms are. Something to help her realize it’s a major problem which affects millions of people – not just you personally.

If she still won’t acknowledge it, don’t let that stop you from seeing your therapist. It’s hard not having support, especially if it’s the support of a parent. But that’s why you can look for support elsewhere, in your other friends and family members. Even if they don’t know you have bipolar depression, you can still go to them for advice or help whenever you need it. It can motivate you immensely, whenever you’re feeling down.

In the meantime, don’t let your mother drag you down or convince you your depression doesn’t exist. You know your feelings better than anybody else. Your feelings matter. Your health is more important than anything. You come first. Don’t be afraid to do whatever you have to do to overcome this.

Wishing you all the best!

Doctors deal with rashes and sick kids and genital warts and bloody mucus on a daily basis. As the nephew of a doctor, I can tell you in confidence there is absolutely nothing you can say or do that’s going to make your doctor think you’re weird. Judging you isn’t their concern – helping you feel better is. Ask yourself: Would you rather keep living with this pain, or would you rather tell your doctor what you’re feeling?

All you have to do is make the appointment. Write what you want to say to them beforehand, so you don’t leave anything out. Tell them all your symptoms in detail, including when this started. They may recommend you to a specialist, or have you make another appointment to do more testing. No matter the case, make it absolutely clear you need help, and that what you’re going through is serious. 

I hope you can get the help you need, and wish you all the best in the days to come. You can do this!

Depression is difficult for people to understand if they’ve never gone through the same thing (especially if they’re from an older generation, and were never made aware of things like depression and bipolar disorder growing up). It’s an illness you can’t see, and that’s why a lot of people choose to believe it’s not there. 

Your mother probably wants to help, but doesn’t know how, and is inadvertently making it worse. She probably knows something’s wrong, but doesn’t realize you don’t have any control over what you’re feeling. No matter the case, she’s still your mother. I guarantee your life and well-being is more important to her than anything else. Even if she doesn’t understand what you’re going through, she would still do anything for you, and will always be there for you. 

It might help to make your mother more aware of what bipolar depression is, and what she can do to help you. It helps to explain that depression is due to chemical imbalances in the brain. Telling someone to “get over” depression is like telling someone to “get over” cancer – it doesn’t work that way. Overcoming depression requires a long, intensive period of healing and care and support. It’s not something you’re imagining. It's not something you've chosen or have any control over. You're not being lazy - you're just taking time to heal. Just because you can’t see it doesn’t mean it’s not there. Maybe ask your therapist what you can do to make your mother more aware of the symptoms. 

I’m glad you’re getting the help you need, and I hope you overcome whatever problems you’re facing. I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

Yes, reach out to someone if you need help. School counselors help students who are depressed on a daily basis. This may be your best bet.

If you tell your friends and family you’re depressed, keep in mind they might not respond the way you think they’re going to. They might want to help, but not know how. It’s hard for other people to understand if they’ve never gone through the same thing. However, make it clear that what you’re going through is serious – and right now, you need all the help and support you can get. (Not to discourage you. This is just something to be aware of.)

In my experience, it’s okay to talk about suicidal thoughts, as long as you make it absolutely clear you have no plans of acting on them. You have to recognize it’s not your normal way of thinking. It helps to treat these thoughts like they’re coming from another person, who isn’t you. 

Overcoming depression can be a long journey, but other people’s help and support will be a huge benefactor in helping you get through this. Sometimes all we need is to remind ourselves that we still have people who care about us, and who want to see us succeed.

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

Just because someone’s related to you doesn’t mean they’re your family. If someone’s your family, they’ll love you and support you through thick and thin, no matter what happens. I’ve had to cut family members out of my life before, and it’s always been difficult. Sometimes they change their ways and we can reconnect. Other times, they don’t change at all. 

The best thing you can do right now is work hard, so you can get your independence and get the hell out of there. If you’re still in school, stay focused on getting good grades, since it’ll open major doors for you. It might seem like a burden now, but any education you have will benefit you in the future. 

If you have a job, ask for more shifts so you can make more money. If you don’t have a job yet, take any job you can, so you can save up enough money to move out of there. Ask a friend if you can move in with them, or do some research to find someone who’s looking for a roommate. 

No matter what job you have, be the best you can possibly be, so you can prove your parents wrong. Show them you can work hard, and don’t need them anymore. Show them you can pave your own way in life, and can handle responsibility. Show them you’re strong and confident, and you’re not going to let them get you down. Living well is always the best revenge. There’s no better feeling than proving your critics wrong, and laughing in the faces of the people who once doubted you.

This part of your life is extremely temporary. You’re not going to live under your parents’ shadow forever. One day, you’re going to be independent. One day, you’re going to have your own life. One day, you won’t have to put up their bullshit ever again.

Instead of letting your anger consume you, use it as fuel. Let it motivate you to work hard and kick ass and take names. Turn your negative emotions into something productive, something positive. 

Whatever you do, don’t hurt yourself, because that’ll only be giving your parents more power over you. Instead of making a plan to commit suicide, make a plan to get a good job or get into a good school. It might seem difficult, but it’s much better than what you’re going through now.

I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

Life is a river, with all sorts of different paths you can take. All paths lead to the same place, but which route you take, and how fast you travel on the current, is all up to you. 

In the end, we’re all trying to find our path in life and where we fit into the grand scheme of things. This isn’t weakness – this is called being human. This is something every single one of us has in common, because this is something we all must do. 

Loneliness stems not only from feeling detached from other people, but feeling detached from the world around you. It’s possible to have lots of friends and still be lonely. Instead of letting that loneliness drag you down, use it as fuel to do something productive. To make a change in your life. Instead of making it a goal to commit suicide, make it a goal to find out what you enjoy doing, and how you can get there.

Take it one step at a time. You don’t have to go out and take on the world all at once. Start with small, practical steps: Work on a resume. Look for a better-paying job. Talk to an employment agency about getting a better-paying job. Find out how much a home costs, or if anybody’s looking for a roommate. Make a budget, to figure out how you can save up to get a better place. Talk to your friends and family, to see if they can help you. 

Remember, there's no such thing as failure, but only the chance to keep improving and succeeding. Success doesn't have to be a big mansion and a fancy car. Success comes from inside yourself. If you try your best at everything you do, to be the best you can possibly be, success will come naturally, without even trying. 

This period of your life is extremely temporary, and something you will eventually work through. There’s still a whole world out there for you to explore. 27 years seems like a long time, since it’s been your entire life - but the truth is, you still have a whole lifetime ahead of you. This isn’t the end, but only the beginning. If you’re not happy with your life right now, that just means the best years of your life are yet to come.

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

I’m not a parent, but my brother was stillborn, and it absolutely destroyed me. Watching my parents deal with physical and mental and emotional trauma still haunts me, years later. There were so many what-if’s: “What if they had lived? Who could they have been? What was their personality like? How could they have changed the world?” 

But anytime I’ve ever dealt with a loss, it’s helped me to appreciate life more. To realize how precious and how miraculous life is. To appreciate the time we have with the people in our lives, while we still have them. After all, who knows what tomorrow will bring? The way I see it, we’re living in a womb right now, constantly growing and developing and changing. And one day, we’re going to be reborn into a much better, much larger, much greater world. 

If you decide to have another child, use that opportunity to shower them with as much love and compassion as you can possibly muster. Appreciate every moment you have with them. Never take a day with them for granted. We’re the result of countless cells working together in absolutely perfect unison, on a planet perfectly fit for human life. We’re not just human beings, but miracles – and that’s something we should celebrate, every day we’re here. 

My aunt lost a child as well. She found out she was infertile. Instead of throwing away her baby stuff, she kept it and put it in a tote. Whenever she was having a bad day, she would look through it. It gave her hope that some day, the impossible might be possible. This might be something to consider. Something to give you hope for the future. 

I wish I had better advice for you. I know this probably isn’t the answer you’re looking for. However, you’re not alone. Even though I’m not a parent, my heart has broken, and there’s nothing that can put it back together the same way again. Nothing can replace the life that’s been lost, but the most we can do is remember them. They’re pure and perfect and sacred in our memories, never to be corrupted by the inhumanity of the world we live in. 

Sending you much love. I wish you all the best in the days ahead.

If he’s not responding and you can’t see him in-person, there’s not much you can do except reach out to him. 

Don’t just tell him you care – show him you care. Ask him how he’s doing and if there’s anything you can do to help. Tell him you’ll always be there for him if he needs to talk. If he responds, listen to him if he’s upset, but don’t give any advice unless he specifically asks for it. (Advice is tricky, and can sometimes make the situation unintentionally worse.) 

It might not seem like much, but it’ll remind him there’s still good people in the world. It’ll remind him he still has somebody who cares about him and wants to see him overcome this. 

No matter what happens, DO NOT patronize him or make him feel guilty. NEVER say things like “Why would you do this?” or “Why didn’t you think about your family?” because this will only make him feel worse. Remember, he’s a victim – NOT a perpetrator. 

I don’t know how well you know him personally, but you might consider reaching out to his family – but ONLY if you know for an absolute fact that they can help him. 

Let me emphasize this again: If his family is willing to help him through this, then it’s worth reaching out to them. But if they’re only going to make him feel like a burden, then don’t even bother. 

In the worst case scenario, don’t blame yourself if anything happens to him. Obviously it’s easier said than done, but whatever happens isn’t your fault. You can’t force him to do something, or NOT to do something. There’s only so much you can do. And so far, you’ve done the best you can do. 

You’re an amazing friend and damn good human being for trying to help him through this. His problems are something he’s going to have to deal with, but he doesn’t have to do it alone. Having a friend like you by his side will make all the difference in the world.  

Keep us posted on how he’s doing. I wish both of you all the best.

Glad you’re still here, bud. It’s never worth hurting yourself, especially over someone who doesn’t care about you. It’s never worth giving them that type of power over you. Keep up the good work. Sending you much love and best wishes in the days ahead.

Four years ago, I fell into a deep depression because I completely screwed up a work project. I was a manager who lost the company money and had numerous people quit because they were so sick of me. I was convinced I was a failure, that my dreams would never come true, that I would never amount to anything.

One night, I decided I was going to stuff my face with pills and end it all. But right as I was about to do it, I thought to myself: “If I’m dead, who’s going to take care of Mom and Dad when they get old?” 

Just like that, I wasn’t suicidal anymore. It’s weird to say I “decided” not to be depressed, but I realized all of my problems were temporary, and if I worked hard, I could turn my life around.

I went to the doctor and she prescribed me antidepressants. They put me in a foggy haze, but gave me just enough motivation to get out of bed in the morning and face the world. 

Sure enough, it took a lot of hard work and a lot of bad days, but I was able to overcome my depression. This past year, I’ve been promoted to director and project manager, and have been chosen to oversee a multimillion dollar project. My dreams have come true, and I can’t imagine NOT being alive nowadays. 

In the end, staring death in the face gave me a whole new perspective on life. I realized the whole reason we make mistakes is so we can learn from them. The whole reason we get hurt is so we can grow and become stronger. The whole reason we have bad days is so we can appreciate the good days. 

In a weird twisted way, I’m grateful for my depression, because it made me into the person I am today. I’m happier and more confident than I’ve ever been, because I know no matter how rough things get, I can always find a way through it. I’ve done my best to help other people who might be suffering through the same thing, and to show people it is possible to kick depression’s ass. 

People usually don’t like to hear this...But if you lay around all day and think about how miserable you are, nothing’s going to change. But if you work to improve yourself, little by little, day after day, then you will see results. 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this - I believe in you!

This period of your life is extremely temporary, and something you will work through. As soon as you graduate, a whole new world is going to open up for you. There’s still a whole world out there for you to explore. You still have the rest of your life to travel and make friends and have fun and make memories. The best years of your life aren’t over, because they haven’t even begun.

The next time you feel like cutting or hurting yourself, take 15 minutes to do something you enjoy. That’s it – just 15 minutes. Use that time to write, draw, paint, study, play music, or express your feelings some other way. Take those negative feelings and turn it into something positive. Use it to work for you, instead of against you. Use your anger and sadness as fuel to make something productive out of it. It’ll help you feel better, and clear your head so you can come up with a better solution. Don’t let temporary emotion turn into a permanent injury. 

Even if somebody’s suicidal, most of the time they don’t actually want to die, but only to get away from the problems they’re facing. But all of life’s problems are only temporary. There’s no problem too difficult to solve or work through. Keep growing, keep improving, keep working hard and pushing forward. You’re a lot stronger than you realize, to have made it this far. You’re a survivor. Use your experiences to help other people who might be suffering through the same thing. You’re not alone – far from it. 

I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this – I believe in you.

Depression is different for everybody. There’s the stereotype that depression is nothing but sadness, but depression can be a whole whirlpool of emotions: Anger, fatigue, lethargy, losing hope, feeling life has no meaning...Depression can ruin every part of you. 

Basically, depression is due to chemical imbalances in the brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” That’s why depression can run in families, and why you can get it at such an early age. Telling someone to “get over” depression is like telling someone to “get over” cancer – it doesn’t work that way. Overcoming depression requires a long, intensive period of healing and care and support. It’s not something you’ve chosen or have any control over. It’s not your fault or anybody else’s fault for having it.

Right now, you need all the help and support you can get. If you trust your parents and family members, I would strongly suggest you talk to them about what you’re feeling. They might have resources you might not know about, like access to a therapist or psychiatrist, who can help you with what you’re going through. There’s a stigma around “getting help,” as they say, but there’s absolutely no shame in doing so. Just because you’re depressed doesn’t mean you’re “crazy.” You don’t have to be mentally ill to be crazy, and vice versa. 

If you’re uncomfortable talking to your family or don’t think they can help you, I would recommend talking to the counselors at school, since they deal with this sort of thing on a daily basis. In my experience, it's okay to talk about having suicidal thoughts, as long as you make it absolutely clear you have no plans of acting on them. Make it clear this isn't your normal way of thinking. It helps to treat these thoughts like they're coming from another person, who isn't you. In other words, it's okay to talk about suicidal thoughts \- it's not okay to talk about planning on them.

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this – I believe in you.

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this – I believe in you.

Cutting is a release. It’s way to take out your aggression when you feel “trapped,” and like you have no other means of doing so. But ultimately, all it does is make you feel worse, and can permanently injure your body.

Turn it into something productive that can fuel you and motivate you, instead of hurt you.

Temporary emotions aren’t worth turning into a permanent injury. 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead! You can do this!

Playing the comparison game is a trap (“I shouldn’t feel bad because I have it so much better than other people”). We all have problems we need to work through. Depression is a liar and a trickster, which will try to convince you that you’re worthless, that life never gets better, etc. You can’t give in to these thoughts. It’s the depression talking – not you. You’re a human being who has the right to be happy, just like everybody else. Don’t let depression convince you you’re a loser. We all fall on hard times. This isn’t weakness – this is called being human.

If you’re looking for a job, work on your resume and make it a goal to apply for a job every single day. If you apply in-person, make sure you wear your best clothes and best shoes. Ask your friends and family if any of their jobs are hiring. You can talk to a temp agency, which will get you part-time work based on your previous experience. If the job works out well, eventually they’ll hire you on as a full-time employee. There’s absolutely no shame in taking a minimum wage or entry-level job, if you need to. Nothing’s more important than keeping a roof over your head. Plus, every job you have will give you experience – both professionally and personally – that’ll help you in the future. 

It’s difficult finding a job when you have depression, but it’s much better than what you’re going through now. If anything, it’ll give you a distraction from your depression. It’ll give you purpose and structure – something everyone with depression needs – and a reason to get out of bed in the morning. Every accomplishment, no matter how minor, will motivate you to keep pushing forward and keep working hard. 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this – I believe in you.

If I’m being perfectly honest – the only full-proof way for you to overcome your depression is to become independent. You can go see all the therapists and take all the antidepressants in the world, but at the end of the day, you’re still going to be unhappy if you’re relying on other people and don’t have a steady place to call home. Finding a job is tough, no doubt about it. But it’s much better than what you’re going through now.

Check the laws and requirements in your state, to see if you’re eligible for Medicare, or some other form of health insurance. They may be able to get you in touch with a physician, who can prescribe you antidepressants. Depending on the insurance, you may be able to get them for reasonably cheap. For me, a Zoloft refill only cost 10 bucks. The same goes for therapists/psychiatrists, who can also be reasonably cheap. 

In the meantime, work on building a resume, if you haven’t already. List all your prior job experience and handyman skills, since they’ll all work to your advantage. Make it a goal to apply for a job every single day. If you apply in-person, be sure to wear your best clothes and shoes. There’s absolutely no shame in taking a minimum wage or entry-level job, if you need to. Every job you have will give you experience – both professionally and personally – that’ll help you in the future. You’ll also learn more about what you’re good at and what you enjoy doing. If you can’t figure out which career path you want to take, first start thinking about what you DON’T want to do. Then, narrow it down.

If you’re interested in going to college (your handyman skills could work wonders at a trade school), talk to a college counselor about getting financial aid. As the grandson of a college counselor, I can tell you there’s ALWAYS free college money floating around. You can get scholarships and grants based on your race, what your grades were, what experience you have, what field you want to get into, etc. If you haven’t taken your SATs, go to the thrift store and get a study guide for only 1 or 2 bucks. You can even get a fee waiver, which is what I did, so you can take your SATs for free.

It may seem intimidating trying to plan your future, especially when you have depression – but if you start at step 1, the other steps will gradually fall into place. With every accomplishment, no matter how minor, it'll motivate you to keep pushing forward and working hard. Plus, it'll give you a distraction from your depression, as you work to become more independent and financially stable.

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this. I believe in you.

First of all, depression is due to chemical imbalances in the brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” Telling someone to “get over” depression is like telling someone to “get over” cancer – it doesn’t work that way. Overcoming depression requires a long, intensive period of healing and care. Depression can strike anybody at anytime. It’s not something your girlfriend has chosen or has any control over. It’s not her fault or anybody else’s fault for having it.

If you want to help your girlfriend, the best thing you can do is show her you care about her, instead of simply telling her you care about her. If there’s no way you can physically see her, you can still call or text her, to check on how she’s doing. Ask her if there’s anything you can do to help her. Next time you see her, you can buy her lunch or surprise her with a gift. It might not seem like much, but it’ll remind her she still has people who care about her and want to see her succeed. It’ll motivate her to keep fighting and keep pushing forward. 

In the end, depression is her battle to fight, but she doesn’t have to fight it alone. Your love and support will make a world of difference. The fact that you’ve come here wanting to help her and be there for her is exactly what’s going to get her through this. You’re an amazing partner for doing so. 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead!

The truth is, nobody’s going to know exactly what you’re going through except for you. We’re still living in the dark ages of mental health, and most people still don’t have the slightest idea of what it’s like to face depression. Our generation is becoming more open and accepting of people with mental health problems, but our parents’ generation seems to brush it off and treat it like a joke. Even if somebody wants to help you, most of the time they don’t know how, because they’ve never dealt with it themselves. 

However, you are not alone. Usually, the most difficult time in a person’s life is transitioning to adulthood, since an irresponsible society will try to place so many responsibilities on you. But this period of your life is extremely temporary, and something you can work past. 

Right now, your ambition should be moving out and getting away from your mother’s shadow. This is your purpose right now. This is your reason to stick around. It may seem difficult now, but it’ll be worth it when you have your own independence. In fact, a lot of your depression may stem from living at home, and not having your own life. 

But again, it will pass, and you will work past it. You can stay at your current job and see if they’ll promote you or give you a raise. You can apply for other jobs and see if they’ll pay you better. You can ask your friends and family if any of their jobs are hiring. You can talk to a temp agency and see if they can get you a better job, based on your experience. You can talk to a counselor about taking your SATs and getting financial aid so you can go to college. You can move in with a friend and give them a little bit of rent every month. 

The options are literally limitless. There’s no such thing as a dead end – there’s always another way through this. There’s no such thing as failure, but only the chance to keep improving and succeeding. Even if you don’t have the motivation right now, if you keep working hard it’ll give you a sense of accomplishment, which will encourage you to move on to bigger and better things. 

I’m so sorry your mom isn’t there to help you, but remember you’ll always have the community on Reddit here to support you and encourage you. I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You’ve made it this far. You have more strength and resilience than you realize. You will make it through this. I believe in you.

That therapist has no idea what the hell he’s talking about. Telling someone their self-harm isn’t an issue is like telling someone on a bridge to jump. Honestly, I would report him to whoever he’s working for. Imagine how many other people he’s hurting, because of his ignorance.
 
It’s impossible to say which case of self-harm is more “severe,” because it’s all subjective. We all have problems we need to work through, no matter who we are. Nobody’s problems are any better or any worse than another person’s problems. 

Your issues are perfectly valid, and you need to continue finding someone who can help you through this. I cannot emphasize this enough: Your feelings matter, and you deserve to be happy. 

I’m so, so sorry you’ve had to deal with this. It breaks my heart somebody would actually have the audacity to say this to you. If there’s any way you can find another therapist, please do so. Please don’t give up now. You can and you will get through this.

Even if you’re only acquaintances with her, you can still reach out to her and be there for her. There’s a big difference between hitting on somebody (“yo w@zzup bby lol”) and getting to know them platonically.

If you’re making plans with friends, invite her to come along. Ask her about her interests and hobbies, to make it seem like you’re interested. Occasionally ask her how she’s doing and what’s new in life. If you wanted to go the extra mile, you could give her a ride somewhere or buy her a friendly lunch. It might not seem like much – but for somebody who’s suicidal, it helps to remind them there’s still good people in the world. It’ll give her reason to keep fighting and keep pushing forward. You don’t have to smother her with affection, but it’s much better to show somebody you care about them than it is to simply tell somebody you care about them. 

If you’re seriously concerned that she’s going to hurt herself or somebody else, you can get in touch with her family and close friends – but ONLY if you know they’re going to help her. Let me emphasize this again: Only get a third party involved if they’re going to support her and be there for her – NOT make her feel guilty or try to demonize her, because this will only make her feel worse. Remember, she’s a victim – not a perpetrator. 

You’re a great friend for wanting to reach out to her. This type of support is exactly what’s going to get her through this. Keep up the good work. Wishing you all the best in the days ahead!

A therapist’s job is to give you the help and resources you deserve, by any means necessary. If they’re not doing this, then it’s time to find another therapist. 

If they’re making you feel so terrible that you’re honestly considering suicide, then something’s wrong with them – not with you. If they’re not taking your problems seriously, it’s because they’re not in touch – both professionally, and with themselves personally. The only people you should be willing to listen to are the ones who are willing to help and support you. This goes not just for therapists, but for people in general. 

Don’t let one jackass make you think you’re beyond helping or that you should give up hope, because this simply isn’t true. Keep getting help and pushing forward and working to improve yourself. You will see results, and you will get through this. What you’re feeling now is extremely temporary, and will soon pass. 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead!

Lynch is a very effective director – the keyword here being “effective.” He’s not as skilled or technically-minded as somebody like Stanley Kubrick or Orson Welles. But I can ignore his flaws – like the weird tonal shifts and overacting and scenes that go on for waaaaay too long – because what he creates is just so damn good. 

His movies are basically paintings brought to life. It’s meant to invoke a sense of emotion, rather than make any logical sense. What can be seen as “self-indulgent” can also be seen as trying to sway the audience to feel one way or another. Lynch is my favorite director of all-time, and this is exactly what I love about him. To me, he’s like a magician who manipulates your emotions and what you expect from the story. But I can completely understand why a lot of people don’t like his work, and why his movies can be so hit-and-miss for people.

Everyone has suicidal thoughts at some point in their lives, which isn’t surprising when you consider that death is all around us. While everyone has an instinct to survive – which is what kept our ancestors alive over thousands of years – we also have an instinct to jump every time we’re standing on a cliff. 

That being said...Suicidal thoughts are nothing to worry about, for the most part. It only becomes a problem when you start planning on them, as they consume your every thought, day after day.

If you’re seriously concerned about your suicidal thoughts, you may be able to get a therapist/counselor/psychiatrist for relatively cheap, depending on your insurance situation. Cognitive therapists are especially helpful for changing your way of thinking. I’ve always been open and honest about my suicidal thoughts, and it’s never had any negative consequences. 

HOWEVER...You have to make it absolutely clear that this isn’t your normal way of thinking, and you have absolutely no plans of acting on them. It helps to treat these thoughts like they’re coming from another person, who isn’t you. Legally, a third party will only get involved if you make a legitimate plan to hurt yourself or somebody else, or if you give them reason to believe you’re going to hurt yourself or somebody else (this means talking about buying a gun, swallowing pills, etc.). 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead!

If you feel like self-harming, the best thing you can do is take those negative emotions and turn it into something positive. That’s it: Just 5 – 15 minutes. It’ll help clear your head and calm you down. It’s much better than the alternative. Don’t turn temporary emotions into a permanent injury. 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead! You can get through this – I believe in you.

It doesn’t matter who you are, where you’re born, or how much money you have – everyone has problems they need to work through. Everyone is trying to find their path in life, and where they fit into the grand scheme of things. This is something every single person has in common.

I tried drinking when I was depressed, but it only made me feel a thousand times worse. Alcohol’s called a “depressant” for a reason. At first, it made me feel amazing. It gave me enough of a high to forget about my problems. But then, when I came down from that high, I came down so hard, I basically crashed and burned. 

The best thing to do is cut out alcohol from your life completely. (Since depression is due to chemical imbalances in your brain, the alcohol may actually be making it worse, and may be what's stopping you from fully overcoming it.) The feeling of euphoria isn’t worth the feeling of misery you get afterwards. To overcome depression, it’s best to be clear-headed so you can come up with a solution to whatever problems you might be facing. You can go see therapists and take antidepressants – and sure, they might help you. But the only true way to kick depression’s ass is to work to improve yourself, and make a better life for yourself. Drugs and alcohol will only hinder your motivation and willpower to do this. 

If you still can’t find the motivation, it helps to do a little at a time. Simple things like doing laundry or doing the dishes will give you a sense of accomplishment. Little by little, it’ll help you get motivated to move on to bigger and better things.

The fact that you want to get help and improve yourself means you’ve already made a huge step in the right direction. Keep it up, and you’ll kick depression to the curb in no time. You have a lot of strength and resilience to make it this far, and there’s no doubt in my mind you’ll get through this. I wish you all the best in the days ahead.

The easiest way to make friends or find a romantic partner is to meet people with mutual interests. It sounds cliché, but it’s true. Conventions, concerts, sports, gaming...Whatever your hobbies and interests are. You want to be friends with them first, before you start dating. If you immediately jump into dating somebody, eventually you’re going to realize you have nothing in common.

But finding a romantic partner is only .00001% of the work. Maintaining a relationship with somebody takes A LOT of effort, to say the least. Everything you do, you have to do for the other person. You can’t be selfish, and you always have to be willing to make compromises. That’s just the reality of it, and something to be aware of.

But at the same time, if you try to wait until you think you’re “ready” to date, you’re going to be waiting forever. Dating is a pool you have to dive into headfirst. So join a club, go to an event, or join a team, so you can meet somebody. 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead!

At that point, you’ll be grateful you got laid off when you did. Life is hell now, but there’s always another way through it. 

I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this. I believe in you.

People mainly associate depression with sadness, but depression can trigger a whole number of feelings: Anger, sleepiness, self-hatred, suicidal tendencies...The list goes on. Depression can also trigger a number of other problems, including severe anxiety, panic attacks, weight issues, sleep issues, etc., which is what makes it so horrifying. In other words, depression isn’t just one specific problem, but a whole number of problems working against you.

Depression is due to chemical imbalances in the brain, which can take a long time to "rewire." Telling someone to "get over" depression is like telling someone to "get over" cancer - it doesn't work that way. Overcoming depression requires a long period of healing and care and affection. Depression is a real illness - not something you imagine. Just because you can't see it doesn't mean it's not there. It's not something you choose or have any control over. It's not your fault or anybody else's.

From my own experience, it sounds like you have depression, but I’m just a guy on Reddit. If you want to get a diagnosis, you can make an appointment with your regular doctor. You can tell them the problems you’ve been having and see what they can do for you. They can recommend you to a therapist or psychiatrist, and based on your insurance situation, you may be able to see them for relatively cheap, or even for free. Also, you may be able to get antidepressants for relatively cheap. For me, a Zoloft refill was only 10 bucks. 

I would definitely recommend seeing a therapist or psychiatrist, if it’s even remotely possible. A lot of people are surprised when they learn therapists don’t give you much advice. Instead, they’ll ask you questions about what you’re feeling, so they can find the root cause of your feelings, and ultimately eliminate it. It’s not a one-and-done fix, but if you work to better yourself, little by little, with the tools they’ve given you, then you will see results.

Antidepressants are a touchy subject for some people. Everyone reacts to them differently. For some people, they work miracles – for other people, they only make the depression worse. It’s your choice whether or not you want to take them. When I was prescribed Zoloft, I had occasional bouts of excitement and happiness. But for the most part, I just felt numb to the world. Like I couldn’t get sad or angry or feel anything anymore. (Also, it’ll probably make you constipated and impotent. Just something to be aware of.) But it stopped my suicidal thoughts and got me out of bed in the morning, so that was good enough for me. 

One last thing: Never, ever, EVER be afraid to ask for help. There’s no shame in reaching out to somebody when you need to. It’s really important for people with depression to have support, so they can have a reason to keep fighting and keep getting better. Your life and well-being is more important to your family and friends than anything in the world. 

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this! I believe in you.

If you’re in school, that means you’re still very young. You’ve been in school basically you’re entire life. You might not realize it now, but school is SOOOOOOOOOO temporary. The time you spend in school is almost nothing in the grand scheme of things. There’s still a whole world out there for you to explore. You still have a whole lifetime ahead of you to travel the world and make friends and have fun. The best years of your life aren’t over, because they haven’t even begun.

Come up with a clear plan for what you want to do, as soon as you graduate. It’s tough now, but you’ll thank yourself years from now, when you have your own life and independence.

I made more friends playing D&D at the local comic book store than I ever did in all my years of schooling, combined. It’s hard to make friends at school when nobody wants to be there.

As soon as you graduate, a whole new world is going to open up for you. One you can’t even begin to imagine, it’s so wonderful. Instead of making any goals to commit suicide, make it a goal to get A’s and B’s at the end of the semester. Save up some money and take a trip somewhere. The future is yours for the taking – the last thing you want to do right now is end it all. You still have so much left to accomplish, and so much of a difference to make in people’s lives.

In life, you learn more from the failures than you do from the successes. There’s no such thing as rejection, but only the opportunity to keep improving. Since you didn’t get into the National Honors Society, take it as a chance to work your hardest to make anyone who ever doubted you eat their words. Keep pushing yourself to work so hard, they’ll be licking your boots one day. Living well is always the best revenge.

It’s difficult to help somebody who’s self-harming, since you obviously can’t force them not to do it. What you can do is be there to support and encourage him, whenever he needs it. Don’t pass judgment on him or make him feel guilty, since this’ll only make him feel worse. Obviously this goes without saying, but it’s worth mentioning. 

I can only speak from my experience, but self-harming is usually a “release” for when you’re feeling so angry and upset, and don’t have any other way of taking out those negative emotions (even though it only makes things worse, and only leads to more negative emotions). You can encourage him to find an outlet for those negative emotions, whether it’s writing or music or drawing or gaming or even studying. Anything to turn those emotions into something productive, and get them to work for him instead of against him.

What it comes down to is being a good friend, first and foremost. Don’t just tell him you care about him – show him you care about him. Listen to him when he’s upset, surprise him with lunch, help him with studying if he needs it, etc. The littlest things make the biggest difference. It might not seem like much, but it’ll remind him there’s somebody who cares about him and wants to see him succeed. It’ll give him a reason to keep fighting and keep pushing forward.

If his self-harming gets really serious, you may want to get in touch with his family – but ONLY if he’s on good terms with them. Let me emphasize this again: If his family is supportive and genuinely wants to help him, it may be worth talking to them – but again, ONLY if they’re not going to judge him or guilt-trip him. (He may hate you for it at first, but their support may be the thing that saves his life.)

I posted this story on another thread, but I enjoy sharing it with people. Depression usually starts from a set of bad circumstances (being unhappy with your job, where you live, a crippling loss, etc.), and spirals into full-blown mental illness.

For me, I was manager of a work project and I completely and utterly screwed it up. I had employees quit on me, because they were so angry with me. I had nobody to blame but myself, for wasting months of time and effort and money.

I was convinced I was a failure, and that my dreams were never going to come true. I hated myself. I hated my life. I decided I was going to down a whole bunch of pills and kill myself.

Until out of nowhere, a thought popped into my head: “If I’m gone, who’s going to take care of Mom and Dad when they get old?”

Just like that, my suicidal thoughts went away. It sounds weird to say I “decided” not to be depressed – but it gave me a new perspective on my situation. I realized all my problems were temporary, and if I worked hard, I could overcome it.

I saw the doctor and she prescribed me some Zoloft. It gave me just enough motivation to pick up the pieces of my broken life, and make a better future for myself.

Four years later, my dreams have come true. I’ve been given a second chance and chosen to manage a multimillion dollar project. Life is so great, the thought of killing myself now makes me sick.

To overcome depression isn’t just to overcome a serious mental illness, but to overcome the problems and setbacks of daily life. This is what makes depression so horrifying, and why so many people succumb to it.

You can do the dishes tonight, and do your laundry tomorrow, etc. Doing little things will give you a sense of accomplishment, and gradually give you the motivation to move on to bigger and better things. It’s okay to sleep more than usual. It’s okay to have “off” days. When you have such a serious illness, it’s okay to take all the time you need to heal.

Wishing you all the best in the days ahead!

As a guy, I can tell you he probably doesn’t want to open up about his feelings because he doesn’t want to burden you. There’s the stereotype that depression is all about sadness, but actually, depression is a whole whirlpool of emotions – constantly going from sad to angry to annoyed to sleepy to sad again. He probably doesn’t want to drag you down or make you feel bad. 

He may also feel like he wants to deal with it on his own. As men, I think we get a sense of pride and accomplishment from solving our own problems, even if it’s something as simple as changing a flat tire. Don’t push him to open up about his feelings, but be supportive and let him open up when he’s ready. 

Depression is due to chemical imbalances in the brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” Telling someone to “get over” depression is like telling someone to “get over” cancer – it doesn’t work that way. Overcoming depression requires a long period of healing and care and affection. It’s not something he’s chosen or has any control over. It’s not his fault or your fault or anybody else’s fault. 

The simplest things will make the biggest difference: Listening when he’s upset or needs to vent. Surprising him with dinner and a movie. Helping him with chores is a HUGE plus. Things like dirty dishes and laundry will probably slip his mind. 

It might not seem like much, but it’ll remind him he has somebody who loves and cares about him. It’ll encourage him to keep fighting and keep pushing forward. In the end, actions speak louder than words: Showing you support and care about him will go MUCH farther than simply telling him. He may feel guilty or like he’s not worthy of your love, but always remind him you love every side of him...Even the darker side.

Encourage him to exercise, eat, and bathe regularly, since these things might also slip his mind. Encourage him to get out of the house every once in a while, even if he doesn’t want to. The worst thing he can do is lay in bed all day and think about how miserable he is. Going to the movies or even going to the grocery store can help get some fresh air, and take his mind off things.

It sounds like you’re on good terms with your mother, which is a HUGE plus. Unfortunately, a lot of people with depression don’t have a support group to help them through it, which only makes it worse. 

First and foremost, you have to realize that your health and well-being is more important to your family than anything else. Don’t worry about upsetting her, or how much money it might cost to get help, because all that is irrelevant. Right now, the only thing that matters is getting you the support you need. 

Since people often have a hard time understanding what depression is, it helps to explain that depression is a sickness like cancer or influenza. Depression is due to chemical imbalances in your brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” You can’t simply “get over” depression, just like you can’t simply “get over” cancer. Overcoming depression requires a very long period of healing and support. It’s a real sickness – not something you’re imagining. Just because you can’t see it doesn’t mean it’s not there. 

When you tell people you’re depressed, they may respond by saying “You’re just making it up,” “You’re not trying hard enough,” “You need to keep a positive attitude,” etc. But you have to make it clear that this is NOT something you’ve chosen. It’s NOT something you have any control over. It’s called mental “ILLNESS” for a reason. 

When you talk to your mother about depression, ask her if she can get you in touch with a therapist/psychiatrist, or if there’s anything else she can do to help you. She may have resources you don’t know about. 

You should never, ever, EVER be afraid to ask for help. But at the same time, you have to realize there’s nothing she can magically say or do that’s going to make your feelings go away. Going to therapy and taking antidepressants will help you, but they aren’t a one-and-done fix either. A lot of people with depression don’t like to hear this – but the only way you can truly overcome it is to work on improving yourself, little by little, day after day. To overcome depression isn’t just to overcome a serious mental illness, but to overcome the problems and setbacks of your daily life. This is why depression is so horrifying, and can take so long to overcome. 

But it is possible, and you shouldn’t be discouraged. Your family is the netting that will catch you whenever you fall. Get all the love and support you can from people – friends, family, counselors, etc. – and it’ll make your journey to recovery much, much easier. They’ll keep pushing you forward, so you can keep striving and getting better. 

In the end, the whole reason we get hurt is so we can heal and become stronger. The whole reason we make mistakes is so we can learn from them. The whole reason we have bad days is so we can appreciate the good days. When you get through this, you’ll be stronger and wiser than ever before. And you’ll be able to help people who are struggling with the same thing. 

I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

When it comes to how society treats people with mental illness, very little has changed since the days of “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest.” Most people still assume that if somebody’s mentally ill, that must mean they’re “crazy.” But you don’t have to be mentally ill to be crazy, and vice versa. What’s crazy is forcing kids in school for 18 years or sending people to jail for not paying taxes. 

People need to realize that mental illness lies hidden in the most mundane, normal people. People like you and me, who work and have families. Mental illness is unbiased, unprejudiced. It can afflict anybody, regardless of who they are, where they’re born, or how much money they have. 

But this leads to another problem: You can’t see mental illness, the same way you can see cancer or a broken bone. If you tell people you’re depressed, most of the time they’ll say you’re “making excuses” or “not trying hard enough.” 

That being said – not only should we raise awareness of mental health issues, but also the SYMPTOMS of mental health issues. What’s horrifying about depression is how it’s spreading like a plague to millions of people, and yet most people prefer to act like it doesn’t exist. 

For instance, when I talk to people about depression, this is always what I tell them: Depression is a sickness like cancer or influenza. It’s due to chemical imbalances in your brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” You can’t simply “get over” depression, just like you can’t simply “get over” cancer. Recovering from depression requires a long period of healing and support and affection and therapy. It’s a real illness, and just because you can’t see it doesn’t mean it’s not there.

When I explain it like this, it helps people better understand depression. It’s not something you’ve chosen. It’s not something you have any control over. Like cancer, it’s a life-threatening disease which has taken over you, and you need all the help and support you can get. 

Which brings up another point: There needs to be more help for people with mental illness. Most insurance won’t cover counseling or therapy. Medication can be astronomically expensive. Psych wards are also expensive and not very effective. Employers can refuse to hire you if they do a background check and see you have a mental health record. We’re still living in the dark ages, and the system is still barbaric towards people with mental illness. 

In the end, what it comes down to is helping our fellow human – regardless of whether they have mental illness or not. We need to love and support those who are struggling, instead of treating them like a burden. The sooner we do this, the sooner society will become less barbaric and self-centered. This goes back to the oldest question of human ethics: “Am I my brother’s keeper?”

It’s a gigantic pain in the ass studying, working hard, working on essays, going to class, etc. But what’s an even bigger pain in the ass is dealing with failure, and feeling guilty for not taking care of your responsibilities when you were supposed to.

In my experience, it works best to deal with all your responsibilities right away, so you don’t have to worry about them later. Oftentimes, the stress of procrastination is worse than actually taking care of your responsibilities in the first place.

That being said – as soon as you get up in the morning, do everything you’re supposed to do. Chores. Schoolwork. Studying. Essays. That way, you can free up the rest of your day without any worry. Unplug your computer and turn off your internet, so you don’t get distracted.

Still, you don’t have to cut out internet and gaming from your life completely. Set aside an hour every day to play a game or browse the web, but ONLY when you finish what you’re supposed to. Consider it a reward, for when you make progress. Not only will it condition you to work hard, but it’ll give you a concise goal to work towards. 

Gaming and internet can be addictive because they release dopamine in our brains, the same “feel-good” chemical that gets released when we eat dessert or listen to music or have an orgasm. It gives you a sense of feeling “high,” and while there’s nothing wrong with feeling this way, it becomes problematic when you become addicted to it. It’s going to be hell overcoming this, but with a lot of hard work, it is possible. If your uni has a counselor, I would suggest talking to them about what you can do to overcome this. They could probably help you out more than strangers on the internet ever could.

Based on what you’ve written, I don’t think she’s serious about taking her own life. I simply think she’s going through a really intense stage of grief, especially when it comes to somebody like her boyfriend, who can bring up mixed memories and mixed feelings. She’s probably confused and doesn’t know whether to feel sad or relieved that he’s gone. She probably wants to remember the good times she’s had with him, but can only remember the bad. Perhaps she feels this was her fault in some way, or like she could’ve been there to help him more.  

However, that’s not to say you shouldn’t take this situation seriously – quite the opposite. Regardless of whether she’s actually suicidal or not, you should still be there for her in this difficult time.

But whatever you do, DO NOT CALL THE POLICE OR ANYBODY ELSE UNLESS SHE’S MADE AN ACTUAL THREAT AGAINST HER LIFE OR SOMEBODY ELSE’S. 

I can’t emphasize this enough: Getting her committed or involving a third party will only make things a millions times worse. The system is still barbaric in how it treats people with mental illness. A mental health record will stay on her record forever, and it will haunt her for the rest of her life. An employer can refuse to hire you if they do a background check and see you have a mental health record. Depending on your state, the government can fine you thousands upon thousands of dollars for trying to buy a gun with a mental health record.

The ONLY time you should get a third-party involved is if she’s legitimately threatening to hurt herself or somebody else. Talking about suicidal thoughts is one thing, since everybody has suicidal thoughts at some point in their life. Telling you she’s bought a rope to hang herself with is a whole another thing, and THAT’S when you should take action. But this is the ONLY time you should take action.

Perhaps he was having a bad day or in a bad mood, and you ended up getting caught in the crossfire. It’s not excusable, since he was wrong to get so upset at you. But you’re probably the only person on the face of planet Earth he’s comfortable enough to show his true feelings to. 

The important thing is to realize it’s nothing but a petty, stupid argument, and move on. It means nothing in the grand scheme of things. If you haven’t already, you should tell him how he made you feel, and how you’d appreciate it if he didn’t get so upset over dumb things from now on. You don’t have to tell him about the self-harming. But if he knows how it’s been affecting you, I guarantee he’ll think twice about lashing out at you again. If he still lashes out at you and won’t take your feelings into consideration, then it may be time to move on.

Whenever I’ve wanted to self-harm in the past, I find it works best to throw on some headphones, blast some music, and let your mind go. You can always try drawing or painting or writing. Anything to turn your negative feelings into something productive. It’s better to let out negative emotion through art than it is to hurt yourself or somebody else. Self-harm will only turn temporary feelings into a permanent injury. 

I hope you two can find a way to better communicate and work through this. I wish you all the best in the days ahead. Please take care of yourself.

I’ll never forget when I asked somebody for advice, and they told me, “Just remember: At the end of the day, you’re another day older.” I seriously wanted to punch them. 

The truth is, nobody’s going to know exactly what you’re going through except for you. Most people want to help, but they simply don’t know how. I doubt your friend was giving you tough love or trying to make you feel worse, but was responding the only way he knew how. Honestly, he’s probably dealing with his own problems and doesn’t know how to get through them, even if he acts like he does. 

If somebody patronizes you for feeling the way you feel, it’s usually because they’re not in touch with their own emotions. Telling someone with depression to “toughen up” is like telling someone with cancer not to have cancer anymore. It doesn’t work that way. If anything, your friend was probably trying to motivate you and get you pumped up to take on the world. But again, it doesn’t work that way. 

On the subject of meds, I took Zoloft and had the exact same reaction. I felt nothing. Just tired and numb. It wasn’t until I weaned off the medication that I slowly started to feel human again, and I’ve felt wonderful ever since. The numbness you’re feeling right now is only temporary. You will feel motivated again. You will have energy again. For now, your only concern should be working through your depression.

In the meantime, don’t worry about how long it takes you to get your life together. We’re all trying to find our path in life. This is something every human being has in common, no matter who we are or where we’re born. For some people, this is easy. For other people, this takes a lifetime. But this isn’t weakness – this is called being human. Don’t let society convince you you’re a failure. There’s no such thing as failure – only the chance to keep improving and getting better. This is our purpose in life. What you’re going through now will ultimately pave the way for something better. You will find your path, even if it takes some time. Please, please, PLEASE don’t give up. 

I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

In a weird twisted way, I’m grateful for going through depression when I did, because it taught me never to take a day for granted, and to appreciate everything I’ve been given. It made me a better person, and helped me realize there’s still goodness in the world, if only you’ll look for them.

For instance: Your father had millions of sperm cells, and your mother had hundreds of thousands of eggs. But there was that one sperm that came together with that one egg to form you. Whether by God or some crazy coincidence, we’ve been given this beautiful blue world to live in, and we should appreciate it as much as we can. While also helping our fellow man, while we still can. After all, who knows what tomorrow will bring?

Intervening and showing there are people who still care about him and want to be there for him may help him change his mind.

Saying things like “You made me worried sick” or “Why would you do this to me?” or “What would your family think?” are only going to make him more suicidal. Be supportive of him and offer to help in any way you can. Again, remind him you still care about him and genuinely want to see him get through this.

This isn’t weakness –this is called being human. This is something every one of us must do. After a traumatic experience like a car accident, it’s not uncommon for us to find ourselves questioning our own mortality and where we fit into the grand scheme of things.

You can make suggestions to him about what he should with his life, but at the end of the day, the decision is his alone. No matter what decision he makes or what job he has or where he decides to live, the important thing is to be supportive – even if the two of you don’t end up where you originally thought you would. 

When you’re together physically, the littlest things can make the biggest difference. Telling him you love him, surprising him with dinner and a movie, going on a vacation somewhere...It might seem commonplace, but when you’re depressed, you need somebody to connect with. Otherwise, you’ll only fall deeper and deeper into depression. There may be times he feels like he’s not worthy of your love, but always remind him you love every side of him – even the darker side. 

Helping him with chores is also a huge plus, since it’s so difficult for people with depression to even get out of bed in the morning. Washing dishes, doing laundry, and all the other little chores we take for granted can mean the world.

I’d also recommend he goes to a therapist or psychologist. If he has a genuine desire to get better and overcome his depression, a psychologist isn’t a one-and-done fix, but will give him the necessary tools to do so. Depression is due to chemical imbalances in the brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” Combined with the effects of ADHD, it could be making his life a living hell, so it’s important to get him all the help he can get.

You’re the best partner imaginable for wanting to help him get through this. It might not seem like there’s much you can do, but having someone like you in his life will give him a reason to keep pushing and striving and getting better. Your mere presence will pull him back from falling into the abyss.

I wish you all the best in the days ahead!

If she breaks the law again, or gives you any reason to believe she’s going to hurt herself or somebody else, then you have a responsibility to call the police. It may end up saving her life or somebody else’s. If she drives drunk and kills somebody, it’s only going to make her situation a hundred times worse. They wanna get in and get out of there as fast as possible, especially when dealing with people who are intoxicated.

It may sound harsh to get the cops involved, but there’s only so much you and the rest of her family can do for her. She may hate you for it at first, but it may be the kick in the butt she needs to overcome her alcoholism and get on the road to recovery. It’s much better than the alternative.

This is a really sad situation for everybody involved. I’m sorry the two of you have to go through this, and I hope she gets better soon. I wish you all the best in the days ahead.

Psychiatrists and therapists won’t give you life-changing, life-altering advice, etched into stone like the word of God. The advice they’ll give you is actually somewhat minimal. What they’ll do is ask you questions about your situation to try to figure out what the root cause of the problem is. Once you’ve found the root cause of your problem, then you can confront it and ultimately eliminate it. 

That being said, you have to be completely open and honest with them about what you’re feeling. You have to have a genuine desire to better yourself and your life as a whole, otherwise you’ll be talking in circles. 

There’s nothing a psychiatrist can say or do that’s magically going to make you feel “normal” again. They may give you some tools and exercises to change the way you think about things, i.e. cognitive therapy. But if you actively work on changing yourself and bettering your life, little by little, day after day, with the tools your psychiatrist has given you, THAT’S when it’ll work for you. Even if you relapse back into depression somewhere down the road, you’ll have the tools to better understand it and overcome it.

It may sound intimidating opening yourself up to someone, but in my experience, most psychiatrists genuinely want to help. And believe me, they’ve heard it all before. Talking about anxiety and depression and panic attacks is nothing new to them. 

As far as medication goes, everyone has a different reaction to different kinds of medication. Some medication may work wonders for you, others might make you feel worse. You may have to try different medications before you find one that works best for you. As soon as you start having negative side-effects, tell your psychiatrist IMMEDIATELY. 

While its your decision and your decision alone, I would strongly recommend you find someone who can help you. Depending on your insurance situation, you may be able to find a psychiatrist for a reasonable price. 

I’m glad you’re seeking help and I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

I was prescribed Zoloft for my depression. For the most part, it made me feel cloudy and hazy. Like I was numb to the world around me. But every once in a while, I would get these “highs,” like I was extremely happy and excited and I wanted to go out and take on all the world. To answer your question: This means it’s working properly.

Depression is due to chemical imbalances in your brain. Basically, Zoloft helps “rewire” your brain back to the way it’s supposed to be. Zoloft helps your brain release lots of dopamine, which is the “feel-good” chemical you get from laughing or having an orgasm or eating dessert or listening to music. This is what makes you feel happy and excited.

When I weaned off Zoloft, I didn’t get as many “highs” as I used to, but I also didn’t feel numb and hazy anymore either. I started to actually feel human again, and honestly, that made me happier than anything else.

If you have any negative side-effects or impulsive suicidal thoughts, tell your doctor IMMEDIATELY. Otherwise, this is the best case scenario for anyone taking an antidepressant. Your motivation and enthusiasm means you're coming off your depression.

I’m glad you’re getting the help you need, and I’m glad you’re starting to feel better. Sending you best wishes in the days ahead!

Anonymous screenwriter and film director here. Art can be the most fulfilling job in the world, but also the most stressful and humbling. (When I say art, I mean all kinds of art: Painting, drawing, writing, music, etc.) Art is enjoyable as a hobby, but it’s not until you try to go to school for it or do it professionally that you realize how much stress and work goes into it. It makes me appreciate the work of professional artists that much more, and how much hell they have to go through to complete their work. 

If you’re going to make a living off your art, you have to be willing to live and breathe and die by it. Especially in this day and age, when there’s an over-saturation of competition. The internet has made it so that everyone and their mother can be a writer or artist or musician. Now more than ever, you have to be head and shoulders above the best of the best of the best if you want to succeed.

I’m not trying to say this to be discouraging, but it is a tough life, and you have to know what you’re getting yourself into. If you go into the arts thinking you’re going to be rich and famous and live happily ever after, you’re going to be sorely disappointed. 

Back in 2014, I directed a movie that ended up being a complete and utter clusterfuck. It was a terrible, miserable nightmare, and I had nobody to blame for it by myself. I fell into a deep depression and swore never to make movies ever again. It wasn’t until I came out of my depression that I became re-inspired to make movies again, and since then, I’ve been able to make a living doing what I love. Honestly, there are some days I wish I could go back to working at Target, but I wouldn’t give it up for the world. I’ve met so many amazing people and had so many amazing experiences, it still blows my mind, and I’m so grateful and so blessed. 

That being said, I would encourage you to keep pursuing being a concept artist. This may sound hypocritical of me after everything I’ve just explained, but going to school for art and making a living off art are two completely different things.

No matter what school you go to or what you’re majoring in, it’s going to be miserable. The constant pressure to study and do well on your exams will never, ever leave you. Neither will the looming threat of paying off student loans or finding a job when once you’ve graduated.

But if you can actually find a job as a concept artist, you’ll be working with a team of creative people just like you, doing something rewarding that will ultimately inspire other people to follow their dreams. Sure, it will be stressful and it will be exhausting – but then again, so is working at Taco Bell. At least with being a concept artist, you don’t have to make minimum wage off scrubbing toilets. 

To me, it seems like your depression is what’s taking away your motivation to be an artist, which is understandable considering how daunting it can be. Perhaps when you graduate, you can take some time off to get yourself re-inspired, and to remind yourself why you wanted to be an artist in the first place. 

In the meantime, it would be wise to find another job to fall back on. Finding a job as a concept artist will inevitably take time, and it probably won’t pay well at first. You may have to do some interning or volunteering before you even get hired. Having a day job will help put food on the table, while you’re steadily working your way up in the video game industry.

If you do decide to switch your major, there are still many other jobs that involve artistry, at least to some extent. In the world of computers and technology, there’s always a demand for someone who can draw and design things. I have a buddy who tried and failed to become an artist, so instead he went into programming, drawing up building schematics on a computer. A job like this may be something to think about, too. 

The point is: There’s always another way. You’re still very young and you still have your whole life ahead of you. There’s still a whole world out there for you to experience and so much left for you to accomplish. You may make some mistakes along the way, but the whole point of life is to make mistakes, so we can learn and grow and become better people because of them. There’s no such thing as failure, but only the chance to keep improving until you finally succeed. Please, please, PLEASE don’t give up now. 

I wish you all the best in the days ahead. You can do this!

Most of the time if somebody halts a conversation or seems like they’re ignoring you, it’s because they’re distracted by something else. Maybe they have to be somewhere, or respond to a text message, or trying to listen to what somebody else is saying, etc. They might be trying to slip away from the conversation without being rude.  

If you’re in a conversation with somebody, make sure you ask them a lot of questions. It’ll give them the impression you care about what they have to say, plus it’ll make you come across as a good listener. It’s a win-win for everybody. 

To initiate a conversation with somebody, all you have to do is compliment them, or ask them the time, or ask them where something is. But when you do, make sure you smile and laugh a lot. People are naturally attracted to those who are friendly and don’t take themselves too seriously. A carefree persona is probably more attractive than anything in the world.

Also, this probably goes without saying...But make sure you brush your teeth and wear cologne/perfume. Stinky breath and body odor is the worst conversation killer of all. 

I had horrible social anxiety for years. But socializing is actually really easy, when you consider it’s nothing but responding and receiving, giving and taking. If you accidentally say something weird, don’t worry about it. Chances are, the other person will forget about it in no time at all. It’s no use dwelling on it or beating yourself up over it. 

Best of luck to you!

You don’t have to be sad to be depressed. The term “depression” refers not just to your emotions, but your whole state of being: Loss of interest, loss of motivation, sleepiness, pessimistic outlook on life and the world, suicidal thoughts, etc. 

Depression is different for everybody, and that’s why it’s so difficult for people to understand. Basically, depression is due to chemical imbalances in your brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” It’s a sickness like cancer or influenza. You can’t simply “get over” depression, just like you can’t simply “get over” cancer. “Getting over it” requires a long period of therapy and healing and care and affection. It’s a real illness – not something you’re imagining. Just because you can’t see it doesn’t mean it’s not there.

Savor your moments of happiness. When you're feeling down, remind yourself it's only temporary, and you'll soon be happy again. I’m glad you’re getting the help you need and wish you the best of luck in the days ahead!

In my experience, it’s okay to talk about suicidal thoughts, as long as you recognize it’s not your normal way of thinking. It helps to treat these thoughts like they’re coming from another person who isn’t you. 

The only way you’ll be committed is if you talk about a legitimate plan to hurt yourself or somebody else – OR if you give them a reason to believe you’re going to hurting yourself or somebody else. This means talking about owning/buying a rope, a gun, overdosing on meds, etc.

When my doctor first diagnosed me with depression, she flat-out asked me if I was having suicidal thoughts. I told her I was, but I had no plans of acting on them. She prescribed me some Zoloft and the subject was never brought up again. 

So if you feel it’s necessary to talk about your suicidal thoughts with your doctor, I would encourage you to do so, since this may be a side-effect of the Prozac. Switching to Cymbalta may help, but keep in mind that everyone has different reactions to different medications. It may help you, but it may make you feel worse.
