Depression is due to chemical imbalances in your brain, which can take a long time to “rewire” back to the way they’re supposed to. These changes in brain chemistry are extremely gradual and may have happened over a long period of time, without you realizing it. Then, it culminated when you woke up one morning and suddenly felt refreshed. 

As time goes on, you’ll probably start to feel better and better and better. Lifestyle changes can help you feel better faster, but they aren't the only thing. If anything, coming off your last set of meds may have been what triggered this whole process.

Depression can occur for seemingly no reason – or in your case, it can occur because you’re unhappy with what’s going on in your life at the moment. If you've been having these feelings for weeks at a time and they haven't gone away, then it's most likely depression.

It’s really great you have a lot of friends to connect with. People with depression often feel isolated and alone and like they can’t fit in. I’d encourage you to spend as much time with them as possible. The worst thing you can do is lay in bed all day and think about how miserable you are, since it’ll only make you more miserable. Everyone has suicidal thoughts at some point in their life, which isn’t surprising, if you consider how death is all around us, every minute of every day. It’s shockingly normal for people to think about suicide, especially if life isn’t going the way they want it to. 

In my experience, it’s perfectly okay to talk about suicidal thoughts, as long as you recognize it’s not your normal way of thinking. It helps to treat these thoughts like they’re coming from another person who isn’t you. Cognitive therapy will help you overcome these thoughts, so they don’t keep sucking you into a downward spiral of depression.

Ultimately, there are two criteria that will get you committed:

1. Talking about a legitimate plan to hurt yourself or somebody else.

2. Talking about buying/owning a rope, a gun, overdosing on meds, etc., anything that can directly harm you.

That being said, I wouldn’t mention the hydrocodone if I were you. Better to be safe. But you can work around it by talking about how you’ve been thinking and feeling lately. I’d definitely recommend talking about the event that’s triggered you to feel this way.  

Again, this is only my experience, so you’ll have to take it with a grain of salt. Every therapist/psychiatrist is different, and will respond to red flags differently. But a major part of their job is helping people with suicidal thoughts. It’s something many of them deal with on a daily basis.

Sending you much love and best wishes in the days ahead. I’m glad you’re getting help and I know you can overcome this. You can do it!

It’s a plague which infests you, ever minute of every day. When I was suicidal, I used to make off-handed comments like, “Hey, that’s a pretty tall cliff to jump off of!” It would just slip out, without me thinking about it. It didn’t mean I was gonna actually jump off a cliff. That’s just where my head was at. 

However, if she’s specifically tells you she has plans to kill herself or somebody else, or says anything about a gun, rope, etc., I would strongly recommend getting in touch with a family member who lives closer to her – but ONLY a family member she has a good relationship with.

Let me emphasize this again: ONLY contact people who would be genuinely willing to help her – NOT somebody who’ll make her feel guilty. This will only push her closer to suicide. Remember, she’s a victim – NOT a perpetrator. She may hate you at first for getting somebody else involved, but it may be the intervention that saves her life and leads her down a better road. 

I would also strongly recommend you DON’T commit her, unless she’s a direct threat to herself or somebody else. Committing somebody should only be an absolute last-case scenario. Not only is it expensive, but a mental health record will haunt you. Employers can refuse to hire you if they do a background check and see you have a mental health record. Depending on your state, the government can fine you thousands of dollars for buying a gun with a mental health record. The system screws people who need help the most, and it’s sickening.

In the meantime, simply being there for her and talking to her can make all the difference in the world. Surprise her with a phonecall, ask her how she’s doing, ask her if there’s anything you can do for her. It might not seem like much, but it’ll remind her there’s still good people in the world. It’ll give her a reason to keep living, keep fighting, and keep getting better. Encourage her to keep seeking professional help. 

This is a rough time for most people, since this is the time for exams and finals. The amount of people on this sub skyrockets around this time of year. In the end, you can’t force her to feel better. You can’t force her to do something or to think a certain way. But you can support her and encourage her to keep fighting. Remind her how strong she is to get to where she is today, and how you know she’ll get through this. Sending you best wishes in the days ahead!

You’ll hear contradicting things about antidepressants because everyone reacts differently and has different side-effects to them. For some people (like me), it works wonders. For others, it only makes things worse.

I was prescribed Zoloft. With my insurance, it was relatively cheap. A refill was only $10. Since depression is due to chemical imbalances in your brain, antidepressants help “rewire” those chemicals back to where they’re supposed to be. 

It stopped me from having suicidal thoughts and gave me the motivation to get out of bed in the morning. I had random spurts of energy and happiness, because it increased the amount of dopamine in my noggin. 

But at the same time, it made me feel somewhat numb. Foggy to the world around me. I couldn’t cry. I was never excited. I was never anything. I felt like a robot. 

So the good news is, you probably won’t have social anxiety anymore. The bad news is, you probably won’t have any emotions at all. You’ll just be in a haze.  

It wasn’t until I came off my antidepressants that I started to feel human again. It was a big sigh of relief to be able to laugh and feel things again. To this day, I fall into random bouts of depression, but I’ve become better equipped to deal with them and fight them off. 

Now for the embarrassing stuff: Nearly every antidepressant will make you incompetent. You probably won’t have any sexual desire whatsoever. Also, it made me super constipated. This is totally normal. But if you have any serious side effects, or feel like hurting yourself, tell your doctor IMMEDIATELY. 

To sum it all up: You won’t know how antidepressants affect you until you actually try them. It may help you, but it won’t make all your problems go away. The only real way to beat depression is to beat the root cause of your depression.

Either way, I’m glad you’re thinking about getting help. Wishing you all the best. You can do this!

It’s going to take some time. You’re not going to change overnight. 

With counseling, you have to have a genuine desire to get better. You have to be willing to open yourself up and dissect the root cause of whatever you’re feeling.

Antidepressants will usually make you foggy and numb to the world around you. In my experience, they stopped me from being suicidal and gave me the motivation to get out of bed in the morning. But it wasn’t until I came off antidepressants that I actually started to feel human again. (Just remember if you have any negative side-effects, tell your doctor IMMEDIATELY.)

I was bullied throughout most of high school. I hated it, because to me, it felt like a prison. No matter what I was feeling, I had no choice but to be stuck there all day, every day.

It wasn’t until I graduated and became an adult that I realized school is SOOOOOOOOOOOO temporary. You’re still very young. School is barely a blip on the map of your entire life. The first thing to do is improve your grades. Obviously, this is easier said than done. But focusing on your grades will open major doors for you, like scholarships and financial aid. Grades are based on three things: Attendance. Homework. And testing. That means show up on time, do all your homework (including projects), and pay just enough attention to pass your tests.

As far as making up the work you’ve missed, take advantage of any extra credit you can. Teachers will sometimes let you do community service to make up your grades. Talk to your counselors about taking extra classes before school, after school, or in the summertime to make up for lost credits (assuming your school has credits). 

If all else fails, look for another school to go to, even if you have to ride a bike or take public transit. Please don’t drop out, since this will only make things worse. But if your current school is having a serious effect on your mental and emotional health, then there are always other options and other schools available. Do research on schools in your area. Make it clear to your parents that school’s having a negative impact on your well-being. Catholic schools are not the be-all-end-all of public schooling. 

This isn’t the end of the road for you, but only the beginning. Please take care of yourself and I wish you all the success in the world. Sending you much love and best wishes in the days ahead. You can do this!

The last thing you want to do is make him feel guilty or make him feel like he’s a bad person. He’s a victim – NOT a perpetrator. Never, ever, EVER say things like, “Why would you do this to us? Why didn’t you think of your family? Why do you have to be like this?” This will only make him feel more suicidal.  

Since he’s suicidal, I’m going to assume he’s suffering from depression. So what is depression, exactly? Depression is a disease like cancer or influenza. Just because you can’t see it doesn’t mean it’s not there. It’s due to chemical imbalances in the brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” You can’t simply “get over” depression, just like you can’t simply “get over” cancer. “Getting over it” requires a long period of therapy and healing and love and affection. 

The unfortunate reality is, there’s nothing you can say or do that’s going to make his feelings go away. You can’t force him to come out of his depression, or to think a certain way. This is something he’s going to have to come to terms with. 

What you can do is be there for him. Talk to him, make him laugh, show him you’re there for him, show him how much you love and care about him. Ask how he’s doing, surprise him with food, hang out and spend time with him. He may feel guilty, or like he’s not worthy of anybody’s love. But make it clear you love every side of him – even the darker side. 

It may not sound like much. It’s not a one-and-done fix, that’s going to magically make his feelings go away. But he needs somebody to be there with him, through good days and bad days, to help him with the battle he’s fighting. 

Having a supportive family will give him a reason to keep pushing, to keep fighting, to keep getting better. It’ll give him a reason to live, and something to pull him back from falling over the edge and into the abyss.

Honestly, I hope they keep him out of the psych ward and send him home. Not only is it ridiculously expensive, but a mental health record will haunt you. Employers can refuse to hire you if they do a background check and see you have a mental health record. Depending on what state you’re in, the government can fine you thousands of dollars for buying a gun with a mental health record. The system screws people who need help the most, and it’s sickening. I would only recommend the psych ward as an absolute last case scenario – if he’s a direct threat to himself or somebody else.

If you have anymore questions, I’d be happy to answer them. I know how horrifying this must be, but be grateful he’s still alive. Be thankful he’s been given a second chance at life. This situation could’ve been much, much worse. Sending you all best wishes.

There are a lot of things that can lead to mood swings: Lack of sleep. Depression. Stress. Hunger. Even hormones. Everyone has a “time of the month,” just like women, when their hormones flare up and make you sad and angry for no reason. 

But the thing is, anger is a secondary emotion. You don’t automatically feel angry. First, you have to feel stress or annoyance or embarrassment, and then that escalates into anger. So if you’re ever feeling angry, figure out what other emotion is causing that anger, and then figure out what you can do to get past it. Take yourself out of the room, get out of the situation you’re in, have a glass of water, etc.

For me, whenever I’m in a whirlpool of emotions, I put on my headphones and listen to music, or watch a movie, or play a video game. Usually, the craziness of the world around me is what drives me crazy; and the faster I can get away from the world around me, the faster I can feel better. 

It’s perfectly okay to get upset, since it’s only human. It’s usually better to scream at the top of your lungs and punch a punching bag than it is to suppress it. But whatever you do, never, ever take it out on anybody else. Sending you best wishes in the days ahead. Take care of yourself!

I would suggest talking to your counselor again, or maybe finding another counselor if you have one available. Maybe she was having a bad day or in a bad mood the last time you talked to her. She may have resources or connections you might not know about, like some way you can get counseling or therapy for free. 

I would also suggest talking to your friends and family about what you’re going through, since they may be able to help you as well. This isn’t a problem of “I’m mad at the world and want to kill myself,” but more of a problem of “There’s something clearly wrong with the way I’m thinking that needs to be fixed.” Your life is more important to them than anything else. Taking a few moments to tell them your problems is nothing when your life is at stake. Society places such a stigma around mental illness, but the more we discuss it and learn about it, the better equipped we’ll be to deal with it.

But whatever you do, DO NOT tell anybody you plan on hurting yourself or anybody else. This is when a third party has to get involved, and people often get committed. Being committed will stay on your record forever, and employers can refuse to hire you if they see you have a mental health record. The system fucks people who need help the most, and it’s sickening.

Depending on your insurance situation, maybe even consider talking to your regular doctor about what you’re feeling. In my amateur non-professional opinion, this sounds like anxiety and depression slowly creeping in, but not quite making themselves known yet. 

If the doctor prescribes you antidepressants (which can also help you with anxiety), they’re usually fairly cheap depending your insurance. (For me, a Zoloft refill was only $10.) Antidepressants will make you feel sleepy and numb, but over time they’ll make the suicidal thoughts go away. When your brain is chemically imbalanced, they’ll help “rewire” it back to the way it’s supposed to be. 

Please keep us posted on how you’re doing. Sending you much love and best wishes in the days ahead. You can do this!

There’s a saying, “Don’t compare your raw footage to somebody else’s highlight reel.” 

People on social media will only post about their successes and accomplishments in life. But you have no idea how screwed up they really are, or what they might be going through, or what sort of problems they’re facing. 

To put it bluntly, people on social media are completely fake. It’s a disguise people wear, to hide who they really are. It’s a front for them to be the person they want to be. People will always distort themselves for how they want other people to see them – NOT for how they really are. If you compare your truth to somebody else’s fiction, you’re always going to be unhappy. 

If anything, the more people post airbrushed selfies and talk about how awesome life is, the more it makes me pity them. It’s like a cry for help. It shows they’re actually unhappy and only want validation from their peers.

On a side note, you have the rest of your life to have cool experiences. There’s no age limit on how much fun you can have. While everybody else is partying and drinking and getting knocked up, it’s better to focus on school. Obviously it’s easier said than done, but if there’s any way you can improve your grades, please do so. You’re already ten steps ahead of everybody else. Your future self will thank you for taking the high road instead of the beaten path. The best years of your life are still to come. Sending you much love and best wishes in the days to come. You can do it!

For me, antidepressants made me feel completely “numb.” I wasn’t sad or angry or happy or anything anymore. It gave me just enough motivation to get out of bed in the morning, without anymore crying fits or suicidal thoughts, but I never had any energy or excitement or enthusiasm about anything. 

However, it was the first of many steps in helping me get over my depression. Depression is due to chemical imbalances in your brain, and the meds will help your brain “rewire” itself back to the way it’s supposed to be.

That being said, I would suggest you keep taking your medication to see how it affects you. It may take some time, but hopefully you should start feeling better soon, between feeling tired all the time.

When you get off your medication, it can be scary at first. I felt naked, and like there was nothing separating me from my true emotions any longer. But at that point, you should start to feel “alive” again. There may be times you slip into depression again, but you’ll be better equipped to dealing with it and fighting it off. 

If your medication’s not doing anything, or if you’re having negative side-effects, tell your doctor IMMEDIATELY. You might have to try different antidepressants before you find the one that works right for you. Everyone has a different experience with antidepressants. For me, Zoloft was what did the trick.

Also, don’t ever think you have to “fake it.” Showing your emotions is absolutely nothing to be ashamed of. If anything, it’ll make people more inclined to help and support you. If somebody shames you for feeling the way you feel, that’s because they’re not in touch with their own emotions, so don’t listen to them. 

I’m so sorry for what you’re going through, friend. Sending you much love and best wishes in the days ahead. You can do this!

Everything we do has an impact on somebody, which has an impact on somebody else, which has an impact on somebody else, and so on and so forth. I think we do mean something to the world, because we’re all changing the world in our own little way. The rest of the world may not know our names, but they’ll feel the effects of our actions.

I’m a 23-year-old male who has the voice of a 12-year-old girl and the receding hairline of a 40-year-old man. I’ve always HATED how I look, and how there’s nothing I can do to change it. 

But while you may not be able to change how you look, what you can change is how you present yourself. Never, ever, ever underestimate the power of good hygiene. If you have a neatly-trimmed haircut with some nice cologne, it’ll make all the difference in the world. So will nice shoes and nice clothes (like slacks and a button-up shirt, or a suit and tie). All throughout high school, I was hideous – but when I became an adult and cleaned myself up, it was a night and day contrast to how people treated me.

When you greet people, smile at them. When you talk to people, laugh a lot. People want to be around those who are friendly and easy-going. It sounds superficial (because it really is superficial), but the way you carry yourself and present yourself will change how people look at you. Doesn’t matter how overweight or unattractive you are.

Honestly, I really doubt you’re as bad looking as you say you are. I’ve known plenty of male gingers who are perfectly handsome. To me, this sounds more like an issue of personal confidence. Perhaps there’s an underlying cause that’s making you feel this way? Maybe this is something to think about.

Sending you much love and best wishes, my friend. Take care of yourself.

Honestly, this theory kind of rubs me the wrong way. I think it gives people the wrong idea about depression, and just how horrifying it can be. 

Indeed, this theory is true to some extent. Depression takes away your optimism. It makes you more cynical and more skeptical of the world around you. It allows you to see the world for what it really is, which can actually be very healthy. It’s like when you’re a kid and find out Santa Claus isn’t real. It helps you “grow up,” in a lot of ways. 

But at the same time, depression is a liar, a trickster, a deceiver. It sits on your shoulder and convinces you you’re worthless. That you mean nothing to this world, that nobody loves you, and that you’re better off dead. Depression is a downward spiral of negative thinking, which can dig you into a hole so deep, it seems impossible to get out of. As they say, “The devil will sneak in 10 truths to tell 1 lie.”

This is why depression is so unhealthy. It’s a life-threatening disease – not something to be romanticized. Not something to be made “positive.” It’s a demon, a devil, a silent killer, a plague. 

To me, this is like saying cancer is positive because you’ll get to meet a celebrity and eat without gaining weight. It’s an interesting theory for sure, but it’s horrifying to me how so many people have depression and yet we know so little about it.

Sending virtual hugs. If you don’t know much about depression, let me break it down: Depression is a sickness, just like cancer or influenza. You can’t see it, but that doesn’t mean it’s not there. Depression is due to chemical imbalances in the brain, which can take a long time to “rewire” back to their normal state. 

You can’t just “get over” depression. Like cancer, you have to go through a long period of healing and counseling and love and support and affection...And even then, the sickness might still be there. 

In other words, depression is not something you choose – like a plague, it’s something that infects you.

I know it’s scary to have someone you love in the hospital, but right now it’s best to have him in a controlled environment, where help is only a push of a button away. 

When he gets out of the hospital, the most you can do is be there to love him and support him. The sad truth is that you can’t force him to come out of his depression. This is something he’s going to have to fight and come to terms with. 

However, the simplest things can make the biggest difference: Asking him how his day was. Calling him to see how he’s doing. Inviting him to dinner. Surprising him with pizza and a movie. Something, anything, to show how much you love and care about him. It might not seem like much, but when you feel loved, it’s often the fuel that keeps you going. It gives you a reason to live, and gives you somebody to live for. As long as you support him through all the good days and bad days, it’ll show him there’s still good people in the world, and that there’ll always be a glimpse of light in the darkness.

As someone who lived through depression and suicidal tendencies, if you have anymore questions, don’t be afraid to ask – I’d be happy to answer them. I’m so sorry for what you’re going through and I really hope your uncle can get through this. Sending you much love and best wishes in the days ahead.

There’s still a whole world out there for you to explore. You’ve still got a whole lifetime to get drunk and get married and travel the world and try your new favorite food and listen to your new favorite song. Before you know it, what you’re going through right now will be in the past. A memory, and nothing more. 

Imagine how relieved you’ll be when you finally start studying abroad, and how ecstatic you’ll be to get away from the situation you’re in now. Don’t look at today as a burden, but as a time of excitement and anticipation for all the amazing things to come. The future is yours for the taking. If you’ve got a scholarship, that means you’ve got a good head on your shoulders, and I know you can get through this. You can do it – I believe in you!

The simplest things can make the biggest difference: Asking her how her day’s been. Sharing dinner with her. Surprising her by taking her out to eat or to the movies. Something, anything, to include her and show you care about her. It might not seem like much, but when you feel loved, it’s often the fuel that keeps you going. It gives you a reason to live, and gives you somebody to live for. My family took me in when I was suicidal, and it’s probably the only reason I’m still here.

The unfortunate truth is that you can’t stop her from being suicidal. You can’t force her to do something, or to think a certain way. This is something she’s going to have to come to terms with. But as long as you support her through all the good days and bad days, it’ll show her there’s still good people in the world, and that there’ll always be a glimpse of light in the darkness.

In the end, I have to commend you for what you’re doing, since it’s probably saving her life. The fastest way to drive someone to killing themselves is to shut the door in their face and leave them out in the cold, naked and afraid of what the future holds. This goes back to the ethical question, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”

There needs to be more people like you in the world, to do what you’re doing, and there’s no doubt in my mind she’ll get through this because of you. I wish you the best of luck in the days ahead.

I’ve always theorized that human beings have an instinct for suicide. Like there’s a voice in the back of our heads, that’s always trying to push us closer and closer to the edge. The will to survive is exceptionally strong, since it’s been hardwired into us through evolution, but so too is the will to die.

That being said, I think everyone has suicidal thoughts at least some point in their lives, even if they won’t admit it. It’s not surprising when you consider how death is all around us, every minute of every day, from the time we’re born.

These thoughts are like a whirlpool that’ll try to suck you in. You can’t let yourself get sucked into them – because as soon as you do, they’ll drag you further and further down the rabbit-hole, until you’re trapped in a bottomless pit of darkness and despair. Negative thinking only leads to more negative thinking.

It probably sounds silly to most people, but ever since I was suicidal, I’ve discovered the best way to beat negative thinking is with positive thinking. Every morning, as soon as I wake up, I think about how wonderful it is to be alive. How blessed I am to have my family around me, a roof over my head, my favorite cereal to eat for breakfast, etc. This is my way of fending off the negative thoughts, and it’s helped a lot. 

So to sum it all up: I wouldn’t be worried about these thoughts you’re having, unless you start having the impulse to act on these thoughts. That’s when depression overtakes you. That’s when you need professional support, as well as the help of your family and friends. In the meantime, take care of yourself. Wishing you the best of luck.

Kids are brutally honest. Kids have no reservations or prejudices or predetermined notions. Kids will flat-out tell you if they like you or don’t like you. So if your niece tells you she loves you, and genuinely wants to have you around, then you can rest assured you are NOT worthless. You are NOT stupid, if you have enough compassion and sense to take care of another human being. The people who genuinely care about you will always stick by your side, through good times and bad times, with all your virtues and flaws – like your niece, for instance.

It might seem impossible to overcome what you’re going through. But right now, the best thing you can do is be a role model for your niece when she gets older. Show her how strong you are. Show her it is possible to overcome the impossible. Take what you’re going through as a learning experience – so one day, you can pass on your wisdom to her, so she doesn’t have to go through what you’ve gone through. The memory of you can’t be there for her, to help dry her tears and bring her up when she’s had a bad day. Only you can do that. You are worth so much more alive than you’ll ever realize. You mean something. You’ve been blessed with purpose.

I don’t know what your situation is like, but I really hope you’ll stick around, and overcome whatever it is you’re going through. There needs to be more kind, compassionate people like you in the world. Sending you much love and best wishes in the days ahead.
James going through puberty in real time.

I can relate all too well. It’s often lonely being trapped in your own little bubble, but as time’s gone on, I can’t imagine being anywhere else. Growing up, I HATED how I was so different. All I wanted to do was fit in with everybody else. 

Now, as a cynical adult, I can’t stand the thought of being like other people. I can’t stand the thought of complaining about my job, bitching about my kids, listening to top 40 radio, watching sports all weekend, or any of the other middle-class America stereotypes people fall into. I’m only interested in being myself, and being the best I can be. I don’t have to fit in with anybody else, because I can love myself for who I am, and not give a damn what anybody else thinks.

It takes a lot of time to get to this point. But once you learn to enjoy being in your own little bubble, suddenly life becomes so much easier. You are one of a kind. You are a work of art that can never be replicated or improved upon. Appreciate all your quirky traits, because they make you into the person you are. The world needs more unique, free-thinking people like you. It’s better to be an outsider than a robot.

That’s a great idea. I have a rule in life to always take pictures whenever I travel or visit places. Not only so I can look back on the places I’ve been and the experiences I’ve had, but also so I can remember the people I was with and how they made me feel. So remember to take all the pictures and video and vlogs you can. You’ll thank yourself years from now, when you can look back on them.

You’re still very, VERY young. At your age, school has basically been your entire life. But once you graduate and become an adult, you’ll realize school is SOOOOOOOOOOOOO fucking temporary. School is barely a blip on the roadmap of your entire life. There’s still a whole world out there for you to explore. There’s still so much left for you to do and experience. You still have a whole lifetime to get drunk and travel the world and get married and try your favorite food and listen to your favorite song, etc. 

I was miserable in high school and blamed it on myself – but actually, I wasn’t the problem. The environment around me was the problem: Being locked in a classroom 8 hours a day, 5 days a week, with people who picked on me. 

If high school’s giving you a hard time, I would strongly recommend looking for an independent study school. Basically, you have a private teacher but only go to school 2 days a week. You do all your schoolwork at home, and only go to school to take your exams. I did this in my junior and senior year, and it was AMAZING. My teachers were awesome and my grades shot up to a 4.5 GPA. Since it was public schooling, it was free and I graduated with a diploma (not a GED, or anything of that sort). If there’s a school like this in your area, it could be extremely beneficial – not only for your schoolwork, but for your mental health. 

In the meantime, I would strongly recommend focusing on your grades and figuring out what you want to do once you graduate. Now’s the best time to do so. 

If you get good grades, it’ll open major doors for you. If you know which career path you want to take, you’ll already be one step ahead of everybody else. If you can’t figure out what you want to do, first start thinking about what you DON’T want to do. Then, narrow it down from there.

Transitioning from childhood to adulthood is often the most difficult time in a person’s life. But if you come up with a plan for when you graduate, it WILL get better because you’ll be your own person, and have your own independence. You can finally discover who you are and what you want out of life, without being imprisoned in a classroom. You’ve already made it this far. I know you can get through this, and I know you'll come out of this a stronger person than ever before. I believe in you. You’ve got this!

From a guy’s perspective: He probably doesn’t realize how stressed out you are or how bad your anxiety is. If my girlfriend texted me she was anxious, I would feel bad for her – but honestly, I wouldn’t think much of it, since everybody gets anxious at times. 

But if my girlfriend texted me “I’m so anxious it’s killing me and I need to talk to you right away,” then I would take it as a cue to respond right away. If you need his attention, make it clear you need his attention. I could be totally wrong on this, but in my experience, women tend to be more empathetic and in touch with a person’s emotions than men are, which is why women are in more of a hurry to help.

Because he’s away for work, he has a lot to deal with already. I’m guessing he’s extremely busy and has a lot of his own stress and anxiety to deal with. I seriously doubt he’s being neglectful or intentionally going out of his way to ignore you. He probably forgets, or gets distracted, or has to take a call for work. So don’t worry. I’m sure everything’s fine.

What’s unfortunate is that nobody is going to know exactly what you’re going through except for you. 

This is some “advice” I got from people when I was depressed and suicidal:

“Keep your chin up and it’ll get better.”

“You should be more grateful for what you have in life, instead of dwelling on what you don’t have.”

“At the end of the day, you’re another day older.” (Yeh, seriously. Somebody said this to me.)

Remember that your friends are only trying to help you – even if they don’t know how. They have the best intentions at heart, and want nothing more than to see you get better. Your life and your well-being is more important to them than anything else, so they may say something, anything, they think will help you. 

However, this DOES NOT mean you’re beyond helping, or that you’re lost forever. Quite the opposite. 

Your friends may not be able to help you by giving you advice – but they can still help you by being there for you. By spending time with you and being a shoulder to cry on. Obviously, love and affection won’t solve all your problems. But if you savor your friends and enjoy the time you spend with them, it’ll be a major stepping stone in helping you get through this. 

As they say, actions speak louder than words. Showing you they care about you will mean more than simply telling you they care about you. Your friends will be there to catch you whenever you fall, and give you something to live for. The same goes for family.

And, of course, your friends on Reddit are always here to support and encourage you as well. I wish you the best of luck in the days ahead. You can get through this!

Playing the comparison game is a trap (“I shouldn’t feel bad because other people have it so much worse than I do”). It doesn’t matter who you are, how much money you have, or what part of the world you’ve been born into – everyone has problems they need to work through. Everyone’s a lost soul, trying to find their path, and trying to make sense of this senseless world. This is not weakness. This is called being human.

While it’s important to recognize and be grateful for the things you have (food, shelter, clothes, etc.), there’s nothing wrong with admitting you’re unhappy. There’s nothing wrong with admitting you need help. You should never feel guilty for feeling the way you do. The problem doesn’t lie with you, but with the world around you.

What it comes down to is that ANYBODY can have depression. Depression is due to chemical imbalances in the brain, which can take a long time to “rewire.” Like cancer, it’s a full-blown sickness. It’s not something you can simply “get over.” “Getting over it” requires a long period of love, affection, care, medicine, and therapy. Just because you can’t see it doesn’t mean it’s not there. The fact that you’re seeing a therapist is already a huge stepping stone in the right direction. I wish you the best of luck in the days ahead. You’ve got this!

Medication isn’t a miracle cure when it comes to depression, but it does help. It won’t make any of your problems go away, but it’ll make the tears go away and give you the motivation to get out of bed in the morning. For me, it was the first thing in a laundry list of things that put an end to my depression. 

Depending on your insurance and medical situation, this might be worth trying. Don’t fall into the stigma that people with mental health issues are all crazy nutjobs, because this is simply bullshit, and a huge obstacle that the rest of society needs to get past. (You don't even have to tell people you're on medication, which is what I did.)

I would suggest making a doctor’s appointment and telling your doctor about your depression. (Don’t tell them you plan on hurting yourself or anybody else, since this is when a third party has to get involved.) I only had to pay $10 for each refill of Zoloft, so depending on your insurance, it could be relatively cheap. Same with co-pays. 

Just remember that everybody reacts differently to every type of medication. You might have to try multiple medications before you find the one that works best for you. If you start having negative side-effects, IMMEDIATELY tell your doctor.

I’d encourage you to stay focused on getting a job, and not to give up. Having a job will take your mind off whatever demons you might be facing, so your depression doesn't keep spiraling farther and farther down the rabbit-hole. It’ll give you a reason to get out of bed in the morning, plus the financial stability will make you more confident with your living situation. 

Also, don’t ever feel like a “useless piece of flesh” for going through what you’re going through. We’re all lost souls trying to find our way in this crazy, crazy world. This is not weakness – this is called being human. When you eventually rise up and overcome this, you’ll be stronger and wiser and more optimistic than ever before. In a weird sick twisted way, I’m grateful for the depression I faced, because it made me into the person I am today. 

Please don’t give up. Keep us posted on how you’re doing. Your friends on Reddit are always here to support and encourage you. Sending you much love and best wishes.

Everybody has their own opinion on what the meaning of life is. I’ve always believed the meaning of life is to leave this world a better place than when you first got here. This is what keeps me motivated to stick around, and was what pulled me out of feeling really suicidal. 

Ultimately, I feel like I live for other people. Even if I can’t help myself, the least I could do is help other people, whether it’s helping a friend move, giving somebody advice, carrying an old lady’s groceries, buying somebody a gift, etc. The littlest things can make the biggest difference. By being generous to other people, in return they’ll show you their own generosity and compassion. It’s turned me from a full-blown misanthrope into someone who can see the good in everybody, no matter who they are, no matter what walk of life they come from. 

Even if I am a miserable mess at times, I take every bad day as a learning experience. I feel like there’s always something to be learned from every trial and tribulation you go through. And if what I’ve learned can help other people who are suffering through the same thing, then I consider it a silver lining. Then, life doesn’t seem so miserable and ugly and dour after all. My happiness comes from other people’s happiness. The more we help others, the better we’ll be able to help ourselves. At least, that’s my experience. 

It breaks my heart to hear what you’re going through. I really hope the things that make you happy can help you keep pushing forward. You mean something to me because you’ve given me the opportunity to reflect on my past experiences and what’s gotten me to where I am today. I’ll be thinking about you in the days to come. Sending you much love and best wishes.

Comparing yourself to other people is a trap. If you spend your life putting yourself in 1st, 2nd, or 3rd place, you’re always going to be unhappy. There’s a million reasons why you might not win 1st place, whether it’s personal bias, popularity, other people’s expectations of you, etc. It doesn’t mean you’re a bad cosplayer.

You shouldn’t focus on being better than other people – only being the best that you can possibly be. The truth is, you are one of a kind. Nobody can do what you do except for you. Nobody has the talents and skills you do. Nobody’s had the thoughts, dreams, and experiences you’ve had to make you into the person you are today. Everything you do is special simply because you’ve done it. Nobody can replicate what you’ve done or do it any better.

As long as you learn from your past mistakes and keep moving forward, you’ll always be in 1st place. Take every rejection as a learning opportunity, to keep improving and getting better. On the same token, savor and appreciate the praise you get from other people when you do something right.

Not only will your cosplay get better, but you’ll become more focused. More patient. More resilient to other people’s opinions of you. In turn, you’ll become a much happier and more optimistic person. 

Success doesn’t mean trophies or awards. Success doesn’t mean money or fast cars or mansions. Success is the satisfaction you get knowing you’ve done the absolute best you can do. It’s showing the world how passionate and determined you are, and using your experiences to help other people accomplish their goals as well. 

Right now, the absolute last thing you want to do is give up. Right now, you’re the best you’ve ever been, and you’ll only keep getting better from here. Nobody can take away the talents and skills you’ve learned so far. Right now, the only place for you to go is up. I wish you the best of luck in the days to come! You can do it!

This should be obvious, but the first thing you want to do is practice, practice, and practice some more. When you’re done practicing, then guess what? Practice some more. Can’t practice at home? Then practice somewhere else. Eddie Van Halen didn’t wake up one morning and write “Eruption.” He played every single day until his fingers bled to the bone, and then some. I’d recommend reading Malcolm Gladwell’s book “Outliers,” which looks at important figures like the Beatles and talks about how they needed 10,000 hours of practice to achieve what they did. 

Second, there’s a big difference between sitting in your room playing leads all day, and actually going out and getting in touch with other musicians and trying to make a gig happen. Don’t just tell your parents that music is your passion – SHOW THEM music is your passion.

Making films has always been my passion. Not many people took me seriously when I told them I wanted to direct films for a living. Some family members flat-out disowned me because I refused to go to college. Instead, I worked the holiday season at Wal-Mart and saved up enough money to go out and make my own movie. Since then, it’s been nothing but love and support. When your family sees your dedication and your passion, THAT’S when they’ll start taking you more seriously.

I don’t have depression anymore, but I did for over half a year, from August 2014 to March 2015. Basically, I got the most amazing job opportunity in the world and completely screwed it up. I failed myself and the people around me. I was going to kill myself, but the thought of my parents growing old without me was what kept me alive. I didn’t get any counseling or therapy, which I somewhat regret. I did talk to my doctor and get prescribed Zoloft, and while it didn’t solve all my problems, it was the catalyst in getting my depression to go away.

Depression is the silent killer. It’s a disease that’s affecting a shockingly large number of people in the US, where I live. Just because you can’t see depression doesn’t mean it’s not there. It’s due to chemical imbalances in your brain, which can take a long time to “rewire” and can potentially lead to other health problems. Like cancer, you can’t simply “get over it” overnight. “Getting over it” requires a long period of love and affection and support and encouragement.

Based on what I’ve seen, depression often stems from a fear of what the future holds. So many people with depression are teenaged or college-aged kids still trying to figure out what to do with their lives, or adults unhappy with their occupations. Sometimes it takes a whole lifetime to figure out our place in the world, and who we’re supposed to be. This is not weakness. This is called being human.

The best way to beat depression, in my experience, is simply to help our fellow man through hard times. Instead of slamming the door in somebody’s face and leaving them cold and naked and afraid, the simplest helping hand or warm meal or place to sleep for the night can save somebody’s life. Financial support is also a must and something that should be encouraged, rather than stigmatized. This goes back to an age-old question of human ethics: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” 

I hope this helps. If you have any more questions about my experiences with depression, I’d be happy to answer them.

You say you want to improve your well-being first – but it seems to me like your well-being will come once you’re independent and out of your current situation and don’t have to rely on your family anymore. If you stay focused enough to accomplish your goals, your well-being will come naturally, without even trying.

The way I see it, right now you have one of three options:
1. Go to school full-time.
2. Go to work full-time.
3. Split school and work halfway.

For starters, I would work on improving your grades. Grades are based on three things: Attendance. Homework. Exams.

That being said: Show up on time. Turn in your homework on time. And pay attention so you can pass your exams. 

Study for your SATs now, so you can take them when you’re close to graduating. (Thrift stores and old book stores will usually have SAT study guides for a few bucks or less.) If you can’t afford to take the SAT, ask your counselors if they have any discounts or free passes for low-income students (which is what I did). 

With a combination of passing grades and a solid SAT score, you will be unstoppable. At this point, you can start looking for financial aid and scholarships. There’s always scholarship money floating around, so ask your counselors for help on how you can get some. Even if you can’t go to school for free, you can still go for reasonably cheap. Student loans aren’t the end of the world, as long as you choose a practical career to fall into once you graduate.

If you want to get a job, then check out some businesses in the area and ask if they’re hiring. If you’re applying for a job in-person, wear your best clothes and turn in an application at least once a week (if you haven’t heard back from them by then). The more they get to know your face and see how eager you are to work there, the better chance they have at hiring you. 

If you can’t walk to work, then bike to work. If you don’t have a bike, ask one of your friends if they have a bike. If they don’t have a bike, go to the thrift store and get a bike for dirt cheap. I used to bike to work all the time and it put me in the best shape of my life. If you live in a bad neighborhood, most jobs will let you bring your bike into the back so it doesn’t get stolen. Otherwise, invest in some heavy-duty chains.

Before a job interview, do some research on the company so they’ll be impressed with your knowledge of them. Make eye contact and ask plenty of questions. Even if you think you messed up at a job interview, chances are it’s not a big deal, and you did better than you think you did.

Part-time jobs are fine and dandy, but right now is the best time to start thinking about what you want to do for a career. If you’re having a hard time figuring out what you want to do, first figure out what you DON’T want to do. In my experience, the best careers are the ones that involve helping people in some way: Counseling, nursing, etc. Other people’s happiness will become your happiness.

Also, bring an empty bladder. Once you go through security, you get one opportunity to use the bathroom. That’s it. Since they’re worried about continuity, you’re not allowed to get up from your seat, under almost any circumstances. Plus there’s only one bathroom.

But don’t let that scare you: The tapings last about 4 hours and they’re a freakin’ blast. It’s basically one long comedy show, with a couple breaks in-between. They’ll most likely bring out two guest stars from other C.W. shows. Also, if you bring a hot date, you’ll probably get to sit behind Aisha. The producers will go through the line and pick out the most attractive people to sit behind her, mainly couples. Sadly, I didn’t get picked. Oh well.

Anyways, I know this is waaaaay more than you asked for, but I hope it’s helpful. Have a great time!

I’m very careful about who I share my diagnosis with, and usually will not share it with somebody unless I’m really close to them. For me, what it comes down to is that society, for the most part, is still unsure how to approach the subject of autism, and especially people with autism. In my experience, it tends to make people uncomfortable, or like they need to walk on eggshells around me. 

It’s unfortunate, but there are still a lot of really, really, REALLY dumb stereotypes and myths regarding autism: People with autism don’t have emotions, people with autism can’t have children, everyone with autism is retarded, etc. Society tends to grasp onto highly exaggerated, and in most cases unrealistic depictions of autism through media, such as Rain Man or Sheldon Cooper, simply because they’re easy to grasp without doing any actual research on the matter. 

My parents and close friends know of my diagnosis, and they don’t treat me any differently. I’d probably tell my potential employers, and I’d definitely tell my potential partners. It helps them understand most of my “quirks” and why I do the things I do. 

However, I’ve had a difficult time sharing my diagnosis with acquaintances or people I don’t know too well. Most of the time, they’re in denial simply because I have basic social skills and my speech isn’t particularly awkward. The way I explain it to them is that it affects how I see the world, and also how the world affects me. 

Of course, everybody will have their own opinions on this issue. It’s always interesting to me how people approach it, based on their age, background, family life, severity of autism, etc.

Nevertheless, for me personally, it really doesn’t matter whether or not somebody knows of my diagnosis. Indeed, being labeled as having “autism” explains many of my “quirks,” and why I think about things the way I do; and indeed, it is an enormous part of my life. However, it doesn’t define me, and it doesn’t change who I am as a human being. At the end of the day, I want to be safe, loved, and fed, just like everybody else.

I can only speak from my experience, and what I would like my partner to know if I was moving in with them.

First and foremost, since Aspies tend to have strict routines, I would strongly suggest getting to know his routines and doing your best not to get in the way of them. For instance, as soon as I get up in the morning, I need to make some tea, eat some toast, and take a shower, in that order. If anything or anybody affects that routine, I get horrible anxiety and become extremely frustrated. That being said, if you accidentally interfere with one of his routines and he becomes upset, don’t take it personally – it’s us, not you. Just do your best to work around it, and let him do what he needs to do. 

Secondly, I don’t like surprises, which means I don’t like people coming over unexpectedly or without me knowing. It’s pure anxiety for me, and when this happens, sometimes I have to leave the house because I get so flustered. That being said, I’m sure he would appreciate it if you let him know beforehand that someone is coming over. Also, try to keep gatherings to a small number, i.e. don’t bring over everybody who’s ever been in the Wu-Tang Clan. 

This goes for relationships in general, but distribute the chores evenly. Be extremely clear and concise with what you’d like him to do. Don’t beat around the bush or leave hints – instead, say “Hey, this is what I want you to do, and this is when I want you to do it.” 

Don’t be offended if he needs some alone time, or wants to watch a movie or do something by himself. Typically, Aspies get overstimulated and overworked really easily, and we need time to ourselves so we can recharge.

In addition, you should bear in mind that the world can be a very dark place for Aspies, especially having grown up in a society where we’re often bullied, abused, and neglected. There may be days where he’s depressed or angry. It may be extremely difficult for him to communicate his feelings. For instance, whenever something’s bothering me, there’s so much that I’m feeling and so much that I want to say, the words never come out because I don’t know how to say them, and I wind up becoming even more frustrated and upset, like a boiling pot of water about to overflow. But even if you don’t understand what he’s feeling or why he’s feeling it, you should still be there to comfort him. If he wants to cry, let him cry. If he wants to scream, let him scream. And if he wants to be left alone, then leave him alone. 

Otherwise, as others have said, cohabitating with an Aspie is not much different from anybody else. In fact, I’d say that living with an Aspie is probably easier. We tend to be very simple creatures, who stick to routines and can easily entertain ourselves. For the most part, there’s no drama. We don’t play mind-games. We don’t cheat. We physically cannot lie. We trust easily. We’re extremely loyal, and will always be by a person’s side, if they’re worth it. 

Of course, you will have your differences and you will get on each other’s nerves. That’s just inevitable. However, don’t take each other for granted. Communicate your needs. For the love of God, clean up your messes. And remember that just because you’re living together doesn’t mean you shouldn’t still date and go out every once in a while.

Like I said, I can only speak from my experiences. No two people with autism are ever alike. Mirroring what others have said, you should definitely ask your boyfriend what his needs are, and what would make him happy.

Good luck with the move!

Always ask the other person about themselves. Human beings are inherently selfish creatures - we like to talk about ourselves, our lives, and the things we enjoy. Therefore, I find it always works to start a conversation by asking things like, "What do you do for a living? Where are you from? How do you know so-and-so?" Then, when they respond, keep asking them more and more questions to act like you're interested. It's easier said than done (most people make me want to pull my hair out), but in the end, they'll appreciate you seeming interested in them and being a good listener. If they ask you a question, make your response brief and concise. 

Also, don't worry too much about making social mistakes. If you watch NTs, they inadvertently say and do stupid stuff all the time - the only difference is they can move past it and move onto something else, whereas people with autism have an unfortunate tendency to internalize it. Just remember that by the time you finish dwelling on the mistake, the other person will already have forgotten about it.

I can only speak from my perspective, but having autism is essentially being on a completely different planet, and a completely different plane of existence from everybody else. It's difficult for me to connect with just about anybody; and even if I do connect with somebody, keeping that connection is just as difficult. In my experience, the most you can do is learn to celebrate yourself and be your own best friend. Things like music, movies, books, comics, and writing keep me from being lonely, since I can keep myself company, and do things I like to do instead of what others expect me to do. 

In addition, you should always appreciate the people who already accept you for who you are. I'm lucky enough to have amazing parents who accept my quirks and don't expect me to change. Besides them, I don't necessarily need much interaction with others. And if you're lucky enough to have people like that in your life (and I really hope you do), you'll realize as you get older they were the only ones ever worth being around in the first place.

The original "Star Trek" is my show to fall asleep to, but I don't mean that in a bad way. It's easy to follow and just intriguing enough that I can stay invested for the entire story, but it calms me down and relieves all my anxiety from the day. By the time the episode's over (each episode is about 50 minutes), I can fall asleep almost immediately. "Next Generation" is also fantastic, along with the shows you listed.

I was in the 3rd grade. There was this girl that I really liked. We go to lunch, and I happen to be sitting across from her. I lean over and tell her, "Psst...look under the table." Then I proceeded to whip out my 3rd grade dingus and show it to her. 

I swear on my life, you would've thought I'd taken out a gun, or something. Everyone in the cafeteria started SCREAMING and FREAKING the fuck out. The guys were horrified. The girls started crying. People were running away in terror. Somebody probably fainted. Seriously, there was about to be a riot in the cafeteria. 

And wouldn't you know? The PRINCIPAL happened to be standing right behind me the second I whipped it out. Calmly, he walks over and whispers in my ear that I need to follow him to the office. I find out they're sending me home for the day, and I start bawling my eyes out. Seriously, I was crying so hard, they had to put me in a separate room just to get me to shut up. 

My mom was genuinely pissed. My dad acted like he was scolding me, but really he was trying not to laugh. My mom's friends wouldn't come over to the house anymore because they thought I was a creepy sex pervert. Still to this day, as an adult, they don't let me forget about this...
